Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to draw the attention of the government to what has been said in the legislature of New Brunswick by the Attorney General of that province with regard to the question of redistribution which has been recently discussed in this House. I will read from a newspaper report:
Hon. Mr. Pugsley, replying to the leader of the opposition, said his attention had been called to the report of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's speech, but he had not been led by reason of these remarks to retract anything he had said in regard to this matter, or to have any doubts as to the strength of the position the government had taken. The statement in the speech from the Throne in regard to the reference of the question to the Supreme Court, was based on the following telegram from the Minister of Railways to the Premier :
Ottawa, Ont., March 23, 1903.

You are warranted in stating that while the Dominion government has not agreed in opinion with views expressed on behalf of the pro vincial government on the subject we talked, it Is prepared to co-operate with you in securing an early decision on the question from Ihe Supreme Court. Having received this despatch from the Minister of Railways the government was resting
easy, confident that the promise made would be carried out. We are thoroughly satisfied that Mr. Blair would not have sent this telegram if the matter had not been settled and the Dominion government having agreed to the reference, will take the necessary steps to, carry it out. While it is a matter of regret that Sir Wilfrid Laurier does not take the same view of this question as the provincial government, we need not feel alarmed at the difference of opinion, if there Is a difference of opinion. Sir Wilfrid may have referred to the protest of Prince Edward Island, which is an entirely different case from ours, and which is based on the idea that a province, having gone into confederation with a certain number of representatives, can never have that number reduced. Sir Wilfrid says we must abide by the constitution, and we say the same, but we say also that under the British North America Act we are not entitled to lose any member because our population has not fallen since the last preceding census by one-twentieth as compared with the population of the four original provinces of Canada. He was not at all concerned because the authorities at Ottawa took a different view of this question from that of the provincial government. It had been their experience to have such differences with the Ottawa people, who after confederation took a very low view of the rights of the provinces. For instance, they maintained that our lieutenant governor was not the representative of the Sovereign and that we did not have the fisheries on our own territory. We have been going on fighting for provincial rights ever since ihen, and in most of the contests with the Ottawa government the provinces have succeeded. The mere fact that we live in a small province is not a conclusive argument against our being entitled to form an opinion as to the meaning of a statute. It would probably be found that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not referring to our case at all when he spoke of the opinions that had been expressed by Sir John A. Macdonald and others. While in Ottawa we were told by the Department of Justice that the point raised by us had never been raised before.
Now, I mentioned this because it seemed to indicate that possibly there may be something more in the way of correspondence between the province of New Brunswick and the Dominion government. I mention it as a reminder to the Minister of Justice who said yesterday that he would bring anything further down. I also mention it because I think it is right that the House should be informed as to the attitude of the government in that regard, whether this despatch from the Minister of Railways and Canals correctly announces the attitude of the government, and if it does, what is to he done in that regard. We have had no intimation from the government that any doubt whatever existed in their minds respecting this matter, or in the mind of the legal adviser of the Crown. But you will observe, Mr. Speaker, and my right hon. friend will observe, that here is a definite and precise promise that the government will take any steps which are necessary for securing a decision upon this point from the Supreme Court of Canada.
The telegram, which I will again read,

Of course, I am reading merely from a newspaper report, but, I assume it is a correct report. This is a very important statement of government policy, which, it seems to me, might have better been made in this House than through the medium of a telegram announced in a provincial legislature. A question of that kind was brought to the attention of the House the other day when my right hon. friend was not present. X think the House is entitled to know what the attitude of the government is in regard to this matter and to learn whether or not it is contemplated, if the provinces demand it, to grant a reference of this question to the Supreme Court, and if that is the case, how does it happen that my right hon. friend has made no announcement on this subject to the House, and that there is not the slightest reference to it in the Bill which has been introduced to provide for the redistribution.

The information which my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) desires is quite appropriate, and I will give him the fullest explanation it is possible to give. Some time, I think in the month of February, we received a delegation from the government of the province of Prince Edward Island, and also, I believe from the government of the province of New Brunswick, which made representations to the effect that they believed they should not lose the representation of population which it was stated they were to lose. We discussed the matter with them and told them very frankly that the government had no doubt at all, that the lines which had been followed in the previous redistributions of 1882 and 1892 were correct, and that, in so far as we were concerned, we had no doubt whatever that the province of Prince Edward . Island would lose one member, Nova Scotia two members, New Brunswick one member and Ontario six members. New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island especially objected very strongly to this interpretation of the law. We told them that we could not alter our views, and after giving the matter our best consideration we still adhere to the opinion which we have expressed in the Bill. They asked us whether we would have any objection to having the matter referred to the Supreme Court. We stated that we had no objection at all, and that we would, in fact, co-operate with them if they would take the initiative, but in the meantime, having no doubt upon the matter, we could not delay proceeding with our Bill. I have had no Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
written correspondence myself on the sub-jec with the government of New Brunswick. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) sent the telegram that was read before the House by the hon. member for Halifax. I have had some correspondence on the subject with the government of Prince Edward Island, and I have just given an order to have this correspondence brought down with the other correspondence which will be laid on the Table of the House, perhaps on Monday. While we will not take the initiative, if the subject is brought up we will be ready to co-operate with them so as to have the matter argued before the Supreme Court.

Mr. Speaker, before the motion to go into Supply is decided upon, I desire to take up the time of the House for one minute and especially to secure the attention of the hon. Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mu-lock) in regard to the very serious condition of affairs existing at the present time and which has existed continuously for some time past in British Columbia. I refer especially to the serious conflicts in the province, interfering with the business interests of the province between capital and labour. At the present time and for some weeks past the great coal mines in the Crow's Nest Pass have been closed down through a conflict existing between the companies and their workmen. The cutting off of this coal supply has very seriously interfered with the supplying of fuel to the smelting industries of the great Kootenay country. For some time past a very serious strike has existed among certain employees on the Vancouver section of the Canadian Pacific Railway. On Vancouver Island, in the district which I have the honour to represent, some of the most important coal mines have been closed off. At the Crow's Nest coal mines, negotiations have been constantly going on between the men and the employers, and to some extent the same thing is true of the strike on the Canadian Pacific Railway. I want particularly, however, to call the attention of the minister (Hon. Sir William Mulock) to the very peculiar and extraordinary condition of affairs which exists in connection with the Wellington Coal Company's mines. The men employed in these mines made up their minds that they would have a trades union, that they would affiliate that trades union with the international union on the other side of the line. For this reason the owners of the mines discharged the officers of the union, closed down the mines, and they have disorganized a happy community of nearly 4,000 people, who were depending absolutely for their livelihood on the operation of these mines. I can quite conceive, Sir. Speaker, how very difficult it is when labour and capital is in conflict, and when negotiations are kept open between the two parties to the conflict ; I can quite understand how difficult it is even for the government to intervene to bring abouf a settlement. But here is an instance in which, because a large number of men employed in a very dangerous industry thought it a proper thing to combine for the sake of their own interests, these coal mines were closed down by the owners and the working men deprived of their livelihood as a consequence. It is important, Sir, for more reasons than one that matters of this kind should be presented to this parliament. In the first place, attention ought to be called to them here because there ought be some authority in the government of this country whereby serious conflicts between labour and capital detrimental to the public interest could be put an end to by the government interceding between the two. When workingmen as represented by trades unions do unlawful acts ; when, for instance, they

attempt to break their contract or when they make unreasonable demands, you hear a great outcry from all quarters condemning these trades unions. Well, Sir, we ought Just be as ready to condemn oppression and wrong-doing on the other side, and to bring to the public attention unwarrantable tyranny perpetrated by a corporation which prevents men from exercising their lawful right to combine in their own interest. Let me say here, Mr. Speaker, that there is not an industry existing in the wide world to-day where combination of labour is as necessary as in coal mining ; there is not an industry operating to-day where men labour under such disadvantageous conditions as to their safety, as they do in the operation of coal mines. I am speaking on the floor of this House, from having a very extensive experience in coal mines myself. I know by practical experience all that it means. There is no industry in the world to-day that is so extensively regulated by government enactment as the operation of coal mines, and why ? It is for the reason that there is no existing industry that lias in its operation such dangerous elements, and that needs such strict regulation and supervision by government authority. Need I remind the House of this painful fact. In the operation of the Crow's Nest coal'mine, less than a year ago over one hundred men lost their lives with one blast. Need I remind the House that less than two years ago, in one of the very mines closed down by the Wellington Coal Company, because the workmen wished to have a union; seventeen men were done to death and buried in the mine. It is unnecessary for me to remind the House that serious accidents have occurred in these British Columbia coal mines resulting in the death of hundreds of the miners. I repeat that there is no industry so dangerous as the occupation of the coal miner, and I say that there is no body of men who so badly need an organization to enable them to protest against oppressive regulations. If the men are to be prevented by the coal mine owners from having trades union organizations, then they would be debarred from complaining of the dangerous conditions that may exist in their surroundings. And, Sir, the day has gone, I think ; the day ought to have gone when the right of workmen to combine should be questioned.
'there is another reason why I believe that this important question should be dealt with on the floor of parliament. Let me point out that the enormous privileges possessed by this particular coal company on Vancouver Island were received from this parliament of Canada. Nearly twenty years ago, this company obtained from the hands of this parliament 1,900,000 acres of. land on Vancouver Island with all the minerals in that belt, free of taxation for ever and with $750,000 in cash to build seventy-two miles of railway. And in spite of this grant; in spite of the enormous extent of this privilege, Mr. SMITH (Vancouver).
this government does not appear to hold one single particle of control over the carrying on of that extensive business. These people, who twenty years ago became the possessors of this vast wealth belonging to the people ; these are the people who turn around to-day and say to the workingmen who have to risk their lives:	You shall
have no combination for your own protection. Although the men did not demand anything, never sought a single benefit, the only reason being that the owner objected to the international connection, it may be a matter of opinion whether the miners of Vancouver island are doing the very best thing in thier own interests by forming such a connection before they are united at home ; but this is their own business, and as for the Wellington Coal Co., they have more than once interfered and discharged men because they desired and tried to affiliate with a Canadian union. Up to the time that these men made unreasonable demands it was an act of tyranny to interfere with their legal and moral right to combine. I direct the attention of the Minister of Labour to this condition of things. I say again that when two parties are in conflict and when the public interest is suffering, it is the duty and province of government to step in to protect the public right. In all the affairs of life this principle prevails. If two men on the main street of Ottawa were to come into conflict; were to question each others rights, were as a result to obstruct the public highway, the chief of police would never question the individual liberty of these two men, but would instantly invoke authority to make them settle their difference. That principle if it be right in such a local matter, is a hundred fold more needful when extensive public rights are being invaded. When the public interest suffers because of a conflict between capital and labour ; because of the oppression of labour by capital, then it should be in the power of government to interfere to safeguard the public interest. I would like the Minister of Labour to look into this matter. I believe the condition of affairs is so serious that it necessitates immediate action, and I would like the hon. minister to take the matter into his immediate consideration and contrive some means of dealing with it, such as sending a commission to the province of British Columbia to take evidence under oath, ascertain the reasons for the present disastrous condition of affairs there, and lay the facts before the nuhlic.

In connection with this subject which has been brought up by my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Ralph Smith), I think it would be well for the government to take into consideration the result of the great industrial struggle which took place in the United States last year, and which deranged the business of that country, caused an

infinite amount of suffering, deprived millions of people of a supply of hard coal, and was in every respect most disastrous. That struggle resulted from the refusal of the operators or mine owners to recognize the labour unions, and it was fought out to the death. At last, the companies were forced to have the grievances of themselves and the unions referred to a commission appointed by the President of the United States. That commission visited the mines, examined the miners and the mine owners, took cognizance of all the facts bearing on the question, and have recently delivered their verdict. That verdict does not by any means exonerate the mine owners, but places on them practically the responsibility for that great struggle and the troubles which resulted from it. The result of that deliverance is that the trade unions are recognized, the hours of labour shortened, prices increased, and the mine owners placed in the unenviable position of being forced from the position they took at the beginning of the struggle. Of course, the labour unions were not faultless. There was the question of the employment of non-union men, and some violence was used to prevent them going to work. The commission recognized the right of non-union men to work as well as union men. But I rise to; call attention to this great struggle and the deliverance of this commission, composed of eminent experts in many lines and one judge of the United States Supreme Court, for the purpose of directing the minister'd attention to a source of information which will perhaps be of service to him in dealing with this matter when he takes it under consideration.

wish simply to accentuate, if possible, the remarks of the hou. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith), because we have very few men in Canada who can speak as strongly or with as much authority on the subject of trades' unions and the actual working of trades' unions in connection with coal mines as that lion, member. But I do not wish to bring into the discussion any extraneous matters. We in British Columbia, as you are probably aware, are face to face with many labour troubles, which are practically threatening our existence as a province, and I trust that the Minister of Labour will see his way to appoint a commission to investigate the causes which have led to these troubles. I am in receipt of letters every day, from all classes of people and from all parts of the province, calling attention to the terrible state of affairs which exists there, and which, if it is not soon remedied, will have a very serious effect on the industrial life of that province. We had a strike on the Canadian Pacific Railway, which began in a small way in Vancouver, and I am told that strike was caused by the refusal of the company to recognize the right of the clerks to form a union. I
do not wish to discuss the question of trades unions. I think we all recognize that men have a right to combine; and if the strike in question was brought on by the refusal of the company to recognize the union, I think there ought to be an investigation of it. Although the strike began in a small way, it may lead to very serious consequences, because a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. The province of British Columbia is a province of great natural resources and is capable of sustaining a large population; but it is not going ahead in the way that it ought to do, and I think these labour troubles have a good deal to do with that fact. I do not suppose that it is necessary for me to say that if these labour disputes existed in the eastern part of Canada, the government would take immediate steps to settle them. Our whole province is practically upset because of them. We have strikes at Fernie, on Vancouver island, and on the mainland. I do not undertake to suggest a remedy ; but I think that if a commission were appointed as suggested, to make an investigation and report to this parliament, some good might result. I am not speaking for any class or any company, but for the whole people of British Columbia, when I say that we must have some remedy, and the remedy must be applied at once.

The troubles which the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith) and his colleague, (Mr. Macpherson) have brought before this House this afternoon are of such vital importance to British Columbia and are creating such mischief out there as to demand the serious attention of this House. As to the proposal that a commission should be sent to investigate, probably that is the only thing that can be done immediately; but I cannot myself see that any good can be hoped from it. We have never had any explanation from the government as to why the commission of the Labour Commissioner who was in British Columbia two or three years ago was revoked about eighteen months ago. Since then there have been two commissions sent to British Columbia at great expense to this country ; but here is a case in which I think all the information necessary would have been in the department and before this House now if that commission had been continued. But I also rise to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Labour to this one common feature in all these strikes, not only those now in progress In British Columbia, but some that hove occurred in eastern Canada ; that is, the refusal of the employers to recognize the unions. The cause of the U.B.R.E. strike on the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has now, unfortunately, extended to Winnipeg, was the refusal of the company to recognize the Brotherhood of Railway Employees. The strikes at Fernie, British Columbia were due to the same cause. The

last ' Labour Gazette ' proves conclusively that the whole trouble is due to a stubborn refusal of the employers to recognize the union at all. Some time last month the Deputy Minister of Labour, Mr. Mackenzie King, went to Fernie to investigate into the causes of the strike there. He went to the company's office and in his report thus described his visit :
The general manager had left on the day previous to attend a convention at Victoria, B. C., called for the purpose of forming a mine owners association.
And he proceeds to say that the manager bad left word with his secretary to inform the Deputy Minister of Labour that the mine owners would not deal with their men as an organization. Here is a most remarkable state of affairs. We find these mine owners, who are combining themselves, denying to their men the right to do the same. As a matter of fact all the strikes in Canada to-day, and all those which have taken place within the last two or three years, have turned on the question of the absolute refusal of the employers to deal with organized labour. And that is the difficulty which we must first tackle. The hon. Minister of Labour has a Bill regarding disputes on railways, and I have given notice of a Bill the same as that which I presented last year, to strengthen the conciliation Act, but nothing in either of these Bills will touch this point, which is the critical point in all these troubles.

The subject brought to the attention of the House by my hon. friend is most important and far reaching. Labour troubles are not confined to Canada, although perhaps the particular part of Canada referred to in this debate has been the special centre of industrial disturbance for some little time. Various governments have endeavoured to deal with this phase of the labour problem, but so far it cannot be claimed that much success has been achieved. We have in New Zealand what is called a compulsory arbitration law, which has been in force nearly ten years. But there are those who contend that it is about to break down. Certainly the employees, to a large extent, in New Zealand are reported as dissatisfied. That measure is one of a strictly compulsory character. The awards are dealt with by a board having legal jurisdiction to enforce them. There is only one tribunal that I am aware of where industrial disputes may be settled outside of legal compulsion, and that is the forum of public opinion. My hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Smith), I understand, wants us to appeal to that forum in the present instance by appointing a royal commission to inquire into all the facts' and lay them before the public. He alludes to the powers and privileges granted to the company at Nanaimo. These lands, he says, were granted by the government some I
twenty years ago as a concession for the construction of a railway seventy-two miles in length, and he contends that in view of the liberality of the government the company ought to be fair and generous towards its employees. While admitting that contention, still it cannot be denied that if any rights should have been secured the railway employees, the proper place in which to have secured them was the charter granting the company its powers and privileges. But if these lands have passed from the Crown and the fee simple in them is now vested in the company, or in the individuals who are responsible for the trouble, the power of any government to confiscate the lands or apply any special remedy is gone, and we have to fall back upon whatever power parliament may be able to exercise generally. A year ago there was a strike at the Nanaimo mines in which 900 men took part. I sent out my deputy, and he was able in a few days to bring about industrial peace. He induced the parties to enter in an agreement providing for peace for a length of time, but apparently that truce has been broken, although we learn it now for the first time. Within the last couple of months the Department of Labour was asked to interfere in connection with the Crow's Nest strike, and the deputy minister proceeded to the locality. The company, however, declined to accept any intervention and there is no law to force them to do so. It is a question whether public opinion will approve of a compulsory measure of interference in the ordinary disputes arising between employers and employees. My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) very properly refers to strikes in coal mines as of a special character. In that I agree with him. Coal is a necessity of life, only to be found in very few spots, so that coal mining is an industry of a monopolistic character, and public opinion would perhaps approve of special legislation dealing with that industry, just as public opinion approves of parliament intervening to maintain the running of railways and prevent their operations being interrupted by disputes between them and their employees. We are unly making a beginning in labour legislation. My hon. friend says that at one time there was a commissioner in Vancouver. Well, a commissioner was appointed there, I think in 1899, but not under any law. He was appointed simply, I think, by the Department of Justice to take note of matters in the vicinity of Vancouver, and later on parliament adopted a Conciliation Act based on tbe Imperial Act of the same name. That Act has been enforced with more or less effect for the past three or four years, but under it intervention is not permitted except with the consent of the parties. When the parties refuse, as they sometimes do, intervention is impossible. Whether public opinion would war-

speechtext:
rant our enacting a law which would give the right to the government to intervene in matters of dispute between employer and employee is a matter on which I would not venture to form an opinion. No doubt there is a conflict of opinion, but it seems to me that there is a gradual educational process going on, and that by degrees employers and employees will come to appreciate any measure that will favour the intervention of disinterested parties in order to prevent these industrial wars.	[DOT]
I am not perhaps at liberty to place on the Table the correspondence I have received from parties toi industrial disputes, it is of a semi-private character. But l ean say this without going into details, that since presenting the Bill now before parliament to provide a tribunal for dealing with railway labour troubles, I have received communications from employees outside of the railway world asking if a similar measure might not be with success extended to them. My view has been that it would be better to p:ace the Railway Bill upon the statute-book, and then the industrial classes including of course employees could see for themselves the exact text of it. and have an opportunity of judging of its efficacy when put in force. Then if public opinion asked for an extension of the principle involved in the Railway Act to troubles in other walks of industrial life, I have no doubt parliament rvould accede to that demand. But it seems to me unwise to force legislation too rapidly. If we proceeded and applied the principle in the Bill now before parliament to disputes between private employers and their employees, forcing it upon them before they were ready for it, perhaps we would make less progress than by waiting. There is such a thing as going too fast, and I am of opinion that no labour legislation will be effective unless it carries with it the good will, largely, of the persons to whom it is intended to apply. Entertaining that view I have no hesitation in saying that my own feelings are altogether against the compulsory feature of the New Zealand Act. I believe that in this country where there is such a feeling in favour of freedom and manhood, the working classes would resent anything in the nature of the legal compulsion which is the feature of the New Zealand Act.
Now with reference to the particular trouble in British Columbia to-day, and especially that in the Wellington mines, I am not in a position to offer an opinion one way or the other as to the rights or wrongs of the dispute. My hon. friend has given a statement, which I presume is his explanation of the dispute. No doubt he has given it correctly, as he understands it, and it may be that he is absolutely correct. But it would be inexpedient to offer an opinion on one side of the case only being presented. As to what may be done to bring about a more satisfactory state of affairs, that is a
most serious problem. There is no law by which we can compel an employer to give labour to ills employees. We may have some control over companies having charters, and who are more or less under legislative jurisdiction, but when it comes to the relations between the private employer and a private employee, I know of no law that will compel an employer to employ or will compel any man to work. At the same time we must use our best offices to try and bring about harmonious relations, and endeavour to induce both contestants to moderate their views and to settle their disputes. It is in that spirit, I presume, that my hon. friend suggests that we should organize a commission to investigate the causes of all these various industrial disturbances in British Columbia. . I can conceive of great good coming from such a measure. Whether the time is yet ripe is a matter for consideration. Whether the public opinion of British Columbia has reached that stage when it would welcome intervention of this character, is a matter for serious consideration.
You might as well extend it to political strikes out there.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would like to interject political questions into this discussion, but I think never yet in this House have we bod any political controversy over labour troubles. We have always endeavoured to proceed ns a united body without reference to party, in the discussion of industrial troubles, and in this instance I hope there will be no exception. We are too much interested, the welfare of Canada is too deeply concerned in the labour question, to make it a political football. I have only to say, therefore, to my hon. friend, that the government will consider his suggestion at once, and consider it as a most urgent matter demanding early consideration. It is to be hoped that if we turn the light of public opinion upon these controversies, good may result.
As to the strike upon the Canadian Pacific Railway, when the Bill before parliament becomes law we will then have a legal right to intervene. It is not necessary for me to anticipate discussion upon that point, but that measure, as you perhaps are aware, contemplates giving the government a legal right to intervene, examine witnesses, take evidence, and submit the finding of the tribunal to parliament and to the country. It is hoped that when that state of affairs is attained, the parties to these controversies will respond to public opinion just ns the parties to the coal strike in the anthracite regions of Pennsylvania responded to the demand of public opinion. They submitted that trouble to arbitration, and now, I presume, propose to abide by the result of the award. The government is fully alive to the importance of this question and will give it every possible consideration.

I,. BORDEN (Halifax). I would remark to the Minister of Labour that there does not seem to be much of a remedy suggested by anything that he has said to-day. We gather from him that he considers the business of raising coal to be somewhat of a monopolistic character, which would justify government interference more than any other business in the country. At the same time he tells us that he is applying to the railways of this country a measure which he shrinks from applying to the business he has just named. I do not regard that as a very logical position. I am expressing no opinion at the present time as to whether it is advisable to adopt that course, but taking the statement the Minister of Labour has made to-day, certainly we are constrained to believe that there is much more reason for applying this principle to the case of a great corporation engaged in the business of mining coal than to any other class of corporations in Canada. The hon. gentleman has suggested that we turn on the light of public opinion, whatever that means. I do not know exactly how the government or parliament are going to turn on the light of public opinion any more than it is turned on at present. The light of public opinion is turned on through the press of this country probably as effectively as it could be done by any other means.
By getting at the facts.

He does not seem to offer much comfort to the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith), who has brought this matter to the attention of the House. With regard to the strike in the United States, I am informed that there was a measure in the laws of the state of Pennsylvania providing for arbitration in case of such strikes, and that it proved absolutely ineffective in the recent strike. Has the Minister of Labour any information on that point ?
No.

Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver could give us some information with regard to that, because it might be of assistance in considering the matter which he has brought to the attention of the House. I know he is well informed on these labour questions.
I am sorry that I have not got that information in my possession at the present time, but I will be very glad to procure it and to present, it to the House.

speechtext: I would suggest that this item be allowed to stand until the arrival of the hon. member for Botliwell (Mr. Clancy), who will be here in a few moments.

Very well, take the next item.
Item allowed to stand.
Toronto post office-alterations and additions, including elevator and fittings, $23,500.
Only $10,000 was voted for this last year. What does the hon. Minister propose to do with this money ?

Representations have been made for some time that the accommodation in the Toronto post office was not sufficient, that the building was in a poor state of repair, and that considerable improvements were needed. A contract was let for this work amounting to $35,000, tenders being called for by advertisement. This vote is to complete the work. The total estimated cost of the work made by the chief architect was $34,413. But after consideration, they thought they could complete it for $33,000. This vote, with the $10,000 voted last year, will make up the amount.
Will the lion. Minister say if the contract was let to the lowest tenderer ?
It was not.

I shall have to ask my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) to lay upon the Table the tenders and the contract, as well as any other papers in connection with the Toronto post office improvements that he may have.
There is no objection. If there is anything further, I shall be glad to furnish it.
I will let my hon. friend know if there is anything fui'ther.

speechtext: Carried.
No ; I understand that the item stands.

Last week the request was made that this item stand in the absence of my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy). I understood then that he wanted some information brought down. I do not know any reason why the item should stand again. Any information the hon. gentleman wants I am quite prepared to give.
