speechtext: Stands.
What about the previous item ?
I should like both to stand because I understand they are both for the same purpose.
Yes.
It is the item for the Toronto post office alterations that I want particularly to stand.
Yes.

When the hon. Minister of Public Works was giving us some information respecting the work at the Toronto custom house he promised to bring down the correspondence. I understand from the hon. minister that there is no correspondence. What he laid before us is a memo.
and a list of prices that are allowed the contractors who are doing the work. There is no correspondence to show who suggested the work should be done this way, or as to whether these prices are fair prices, or who assumed the responsibility of advising the hon. minister to do the work on these terms and conditions. Did the local architect, Mr. Curry, advise that these prices should be paid to Messrs Brown & Love to do the work under these conditions without asking for bids from other reputable contractors In the city ?

As I explained on a previous occasion, reports received in the department showed that this building was really in a very dangerous state. The chief architect himself went to Toronto, discussed the whole matter, made this arrangement and took the responsibility of it, and I endorse what lie did. I believe everything is proper and that the prices are reasonable.
Did he. have any consultation with the local architect up there ?
Yes.
Is there any correspondence between the local architect and the chief architect ?
No, the chief architect was on the ground himself.
From whom was the report received as to the critical condition of the building ? Was it from the local architect 7
Yes.
The local architect reported that the building was in a critical condition, the chief architect went up, and between them they gave out a contract to have the work done ?
Yes.

Without asking for bids to do the work from other contractors ?
Nortli-west Territories-Court house, lock-up and police accommodation, &c., $1,500.
Where is this court house ?

This is a general vote for the territories. The previous vote was $1,000 and it has been increased by $500. This is found necessary owing to the increased number of buildings, and these buildings, being of wood, the vote was not found sufficient to keep them in repair.
Dominion public buildings-renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $5,000.
What is the explanation of the increase ?

There is only one explanation ; we are asking $1,000 more because of the increased number of buildings in the territories. The $4,000 previously voted was found to be insufficient. Our property is being destroyed owing to the fact of our not having money enough to look after it and repair It properly.
Maeleod court house, $10,000.

May I ask the hon._ minister what public building there is now' at Maeleod ? There is a public building of some nature but whether it is owned by the territories or the Dominion I do not know; yet, when I stop to think it must of necessity belong to the Dominion.
My information is that there is no public building except the one under construction now; that is the new court house.

I do not know whether Maeleod is an incorporated town or not. I was only there once In my life. There is a brick building of fairly considerable size and I assume it must be a public building and a government building.

I know the building myself that the kon. gentleman refers to and it is a very good hall. It must belong to the municipality. Tlie deputy informs me that we have no public building there except this one which is under construction. This building is under construction and under contract and this amount is to complete the contract.

If my recollection is right, Maeleod was one of the first towns in the North-west Territory and it hardly seems conceivable that there have been no public buildings at that place for the transaction of public business outside of the buildings of the Mounted Police force. Can it be possible that in connection with the administration of justice there is no public building at Maeleod ?
They had a rented building previously.
Which building was it that was rented ? Was it the public hall ?
There is a contract, I suppose for this work ?
Yes.
[DOT] What is the total amount expended, and what will be the entire cost ?
The amount of the contract is $13,973, and printing and advertising, heating, furniture and fixtures, electric wiring, fenc-
ing, sidewalks, clerk of works and incidental expenses, bringing the total to $21,735. The chief architect informs me that this is quite sufficient to complete the whole building.
The contract has been let ?

Yes, the contract has been let to the lowest tenderer.
Red Deer-Court house, lock-up, &c., and land office, $10,000.
Mr. BENNETT!" Has the contract been made for this building ?
The contract has not been let.
Has the site been purchased ?

The site has been purchased for $830. One of the causes of delay was that there was some question as to whether it would be a wooden or a brick building, and there may be a further report as to whether the building will be of wood or of brick. The chief architect thinks that a suitable building can be put up for this amount.
One would come to the conclusion that there should be a considerable difference between the cost of a wooden building and the cost of a brick building.

The chief architect informs me that on a rough estimate there would be a difference of $6,000 or $7,000. This estimate would be for a wooden building but if it were decided to be in the public interest to put up a brick building we would have to ask a further amount of $6,000 or $7,000.

This is practically voting an appropriation in blank Neither the minister or the chief architect appear to have decided whether they will put up a wooden or a brick building. Now when we are voting money in this way we should know as nearly as possible what the character of the building is to be and what it will cost. I do not think that the minister himself will contend that the principle upon which he asks this vote is a proper principle.

The hon. gentleman has misunderstood me. I said this estimate was made for a wooden building and the vote was for a wooden building, but there was a petition asking for a brick building. I told the hon. gentleman that a report had not been made on that, but if it were in the public interest to erect a brick building we would have to ask for a further vote. None of this money will be spent for a brick building without a further vote being asked and an explanation givem.

JH'. CLANCY. Do I understand the minister to say that none of this money will be spent until he comes back to the House for a vote under the changed conditions.

I do not think it would be right for me to ask a vote for a wooden building and then if we decided to put up a brick building which would cost a great deal more, to make that change without informing the House.

Then I misunderstood the hon. gentleman.
Yorkton court house and jail, $5,500.
Is this let by contract to the lowest tenderer ?
The work is under construction and it was let to the lowest tenderer at $8,760. The total cost is estimated at $14,529. There will be the heating to do and the furniture to put in and so on.

I have already told the Minister of Public Works that the money of the people was not properly spent throughout the country and here is a case in point. You are asking a vote of $10,000 for a court house, lock-ups, &c., and land office at Red Deer; and $5,500 for a court house and jail at Yorkton. Now if you can afford to spend $10,000 to build a post office in a town like L'Assomption with a population of 1,605 and $10,000 in Thetford Mines;; it would only seem reasonable that you should expend more money for these important public buildings in growing towns in the North-west Territories. There does not seem to be any system about the thing. The government does not seem to have any rule to guide it in these matters.
Dominion public buildings generally, $34,500.
What does this item apply to ?
It is to cover miscellaneous items of expenditure, chiefly in the architect's office in connection with public buildings throughout the Dominion.
Does any portion of this vote go to the armoury at Sussex in the county of King's, N.B. ?

If the chief architect had occasion to do any work in connection with that building, or to send any person to inspect it, that expense will be paid out of this vote. This applies particularly to the head office staff of the chief architect. The subject my hon. friend refers to will come up under another vote.
Has the $5,000 which was voted last year been spent ? If not, how much of it has been spent ?
Last year there was a supplementary vote of $2,000. The total amount expended was over $7,000. We thought we might manage next year with $5,000.
Do I understand that there was an over-expenditure of $2,000 last year?

A supplementary vote was taken to cover that amount. I cannot tell my hon. friend just what the amount of the expenditure for the present year is; but a vote of $5,000 was taken, and I hope we shall be able to remain within that amount.
I am anxious to kuow the reason for the somewhat exceptional expenditure of last year.
There seems to have been an increased amount required for telegraph stations, &c.

I do not quite understand the reason for these different items :	public buildings in Nova Scotia,
public buildings in New Brunswick, public buildings in the maritime provinces, public buildings in Quebec, public buildings in Ontario, public buildings in Manitoba, public buildings in the North-west Territories, public buildings in British Columbia, and then public buildings generally. I suppose this arrangement is a relic of some old system ; but I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works whether he does think it a very business like way of bringing down the estimates. We might have half a dozen more items for public buildings in detail.

My hon. friend seems to take the view I did myself when I came to look at these estimates. I suppose this arrangement was forced on the department by parliament wanting to know everything in detail. If one vote were taken, including all these items, there might be a feeling that some of the provinces did not receive the attention they were entitled to. That was perhaps the first reason for the system. There is also some advantage to the department in giving the items in detail. If the officials of the department were allowed to draw on a general vote, instead of being limited by these detailed votes, the expenditure might be thought excessive.

With regard to the item under consideration, the expenditure last year was $7,132.33. Out of this there was expended for stationery for the office $2,482.80. This does seem to me to be an extraordinary sum for stationery, and perhaps the hon. minister can give some explanation of it.

Not having been long connected with the department, lam unable to say whether that item is excessive or not. However, on COD-



m
sultation with the deputy minister, we think we can make the total for this year $5,000, instead of $7,000, and also for next year, for which this vote is asked. X may say that the stationery is all purchased through the government Stationery Department.

I can quite understand that the hon. gentieman, in the short time he has been in the department, may not have mastered all these details, but it seems to me that his deputy should be able to give him the reasons for this heavy expenditure.
Over a thousand dollars seems a great deal for photographic supplies, and it seems a little strange that they should come under the head of public buildings generally.
These photographers are all in connection with public buildings.
Are you making a collection of the photographs of public buildings ?

These photographs really save a great deal of expense and loss of time, as they save the copying of plans and also travelling expenses. The engineers and architects are photographers themselves and save the department the expense of sending photographers to do the work.

A local newspaper suggested, respecting the hon. gentleman's predecessor, that he was very active and ambitious and could do all the work of all the other departments, and the Toronto ' Globe ' suggested that he thought his colleagues had nothing to do but sit in front of government buildings and have their photographs taken. Would there be any connection between that suggestion and this item ? We are certainly entitled to fuller information than we have had.
Salaries to resident clerk of works, $10,500.
Is the salary of Mr. McLean included in this ?
This vote is for the resident permanent clerks. The gentleman my hon. friend refers to was only clerk of works while the work was going on, and he is paid out of a special vote.
What are the duties of these officers ? Are they permanent officers of the department stationed at different points ?

There are three in Quebec, three at Ottawa, two in Manitoba, two in British Columbia, one in New Brunswick, and none in Nova Scotia. My deputy informs me that in Nova Scotia the chief engineer there acts as clerk of works. These men are practi-1
csilly the representatives of the department in these various provinces. They look after the public buildings and report and are held responsible for the different expenditures thereon.

Are these men sent about from place to place ? I understand that there are local clerks employed as well where public works are being done. If these men are not architects, their position would seem to be merely ornamental.

These men act as agents for the department in the various provinces and besides there are local clerks of works who act as foremen and see that everything is done according to specifications, These men were appointed previous to this government taking office and no changes have been made, and my deputy informs me that they render valuable service. They are supposed to be practical men and well qualified for the positions they hold. As I have tried to explain, this does not refer to the clerks of works, foremen, or whatever you call them in charge of the works under construction. These are representatives of the department in the various provinces. I do not know that there has been any reason to find fault with the qualifications of these men.

The hon. minister will see that I was not finding fault,but trying to gain information with respect to representatives of the Public Works Department who may be necessary, as the hon. gentleman states, in places a long distance from the capital, and who stand between the engineer acting for the department and the clerks of a works locally. I simply asked if they were architects, and, whether, if called upon to discharge the duties of architects, they would be able to do so.
The officers referred to are not architects. Of course, you could not engage architects at the salaries paid to these men.

I would like to know upon what principle these local men are appointed. Is a mason selected in the case of a building to be constructed of stone, a carpenter or master builder for wooden structure, and so on ?

The policy of the department has been to take practical men. I myself favour, as far as possible, the appointment of architects. But there is no fixed rule. The clerk of works is recommended by the member for the riding. Practical men are appointed, who are supposed to be qualified, to see that the specifications of the architects on which the contracts are taken, are carried out.
Is there a resident engineer in each province where these clerks are at work ?

There are in the provinces several engineers in the different branches of the department, in addition to these men. The staff for which this vote is taken have duties altogether connected with building.
Public buildings generally-construction of armouries, $9,000.
Perhaps the hon. minister can tell me now whether any portion of this is being expended on the armoury at Sussex, and if so, how much, and for what purpose ?
Yes, I And details of expenditure during the current year, 1902-3, amounting to $2,276.17.
Is that expenditure up to the present time ?
No, up to the 1st of January last.
Would the hon. minister kindly give me the details of that expenditure ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) can hardly expect the full details. If the hon. gentleman moves for a return, I will bring down all the details in the usual way.
Will the hon. minister allow this item to stand until that information is given ?
I do not see any objection in allowing the item to stand.	*

I wish the opportunity to discuss this matter. There are some things in connection with it that ought to be brought to the attention of the department. If that had been done before perhaps these things might have been stopped.

I do not desire to prevent the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) from having every opportunity now or on a future occasion of discussing this matter. But he will see that the expenditure he wishes to discuss is only a small portion of this whole item. When I bring down the details, the hon. gentleman will have an opportunity, for the item can be passed with that understanding. Besides there will be, in the supplementary estimates, a special item for the Sussex armoury and the matter can be discusssed on that item.
I do not see why the item should not stand.

I have tried to explain to my hon. friend- there are fourteen public buildings covered by the item we are now discussing ; hon. gentlemen on either side may wish information with regard to any of these matters 31i
and I am ready to give them all I can. It would be more convenient for the committee to give whatever information is required now and allow the item to pass. The hon. gentleman can reserve his right to discuss the matter on some other item of these estimates, or the item in the supplementary estimates will afford him an opportunity.
The only thing I desire is to bring to the attention of the department the condition of affairs in connection with the Sussex armoury.
I guarantee my hon. friend that he will have an opportunity to do so.
I would ask the hon. minister why the improvements in connection with the armoury in the public building in Brampton were not gone on with, as promised.

I have consulted the deputy minister, who informs me that the matter referred to by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has not come to the attention of the Public Works Department. It may be an item in connection with the Militia Department, and perhaps my hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) may be able to answer.
I do not remember it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden).

speechtext: I brought this matter up the year before last, and I will read what was then said for the benefit of the minister :
I understand there is a proposal to fit up a room in a public building for the armoury.
Have tenders been asked for that purpose ?
It is a small work, and we shall not ask for tenders. I think it will cost about $1,000.
Will that be under the charge of the hon. gentleman's department ?

The request has been made to us.
So there must have been a request in the department for the expenditure of that money.
Is the expenditure asked for in connection with the public building there, or with the armoury ?
It is a joint building, partly a public building and partly an armoury.
That will come up under another item, I will try and get the information.

Will the minister lay on the Table for a general discussion of armouries hereafter, a return to the request

that was made to the department concerning the expenditure of that money ?
I will bring that down on Monday.

Before this item passes, 1 want it distinctly understood that this return will be brought down containing this information, and that I may have an opportunity to discuss this question under any other item of the hon. gentleman's estimates.
I promise to give the hon. gentleman ,id opportunity of discussing it, after the report is brought down, on any other item in the estimates.
The minister has mentioned that several armouries are under construction. Perhaps it would be well to tell us in a general way where they are, and the amounts expended.

I will give the names of all the places where the last vote has been expended, that is where the largest amounts have been paid. Small amounts under $100 are not referred to. Baddeck, N.S., $1,398; a small item for the Halifax drill hall; Middleton, N.S., $5,410; Sussex, N.B., $2,110: Woodstock, N.B., $780; Brockville, Ont., $3,150; a small amount for the Brantford armoury; St. Thomas. Ont., $490; Windsor, a small amount. Then there are new armouries; Kaslo, B.C., $3,504; Kamloops. $6,004: Nelson, $7,703: Revelstoke, $0,439, making a total of $37,126.

I would like the Minister of Public Works to give us some information as to the status of those clerks who seem to have permanent positions, but are not classified. The leader of the opposition asked a moment ago if they were permanent clerks. Now there are some cases where they seem to be in the outside service, and some of them are located in Ottawa, but they do not appear in the civil service list. We ought to know something of the positions they occupy.

The hon. gentleman is right. I think under the Civil Service Act they are not recognized as permanent officials, but they are recognized as such in the departments. Most of them have held their positions for a long time. Not all of them are even appointed by Order in Council: but in the department they are considered as permanent, and some of them are responsible representatives of the department in the various provinces. It is in that sense that I used the words 'permanent employees'; but according to the Civil Service Act they would not come under that term.

It would be very convenient if these officials were classified in
some manner so that we could know where to find them. I have no doubt the hon. gentleman is following the course adopted by a preceding government, but that is uo reason why it should be continued. The hon. gentleman will see how inconvenient it is to find in the Auditor General's report that sums are being paid to these officers, while we find no mention of them in the civil service list; there is no means of tracing them, no means of ascertaining what position they occupy. There should be some class in which we would be able to find all the persons who have permanent employment in the department, whether in the inside sei'vice or the outside service.

I will take a note of the observations of the hon. gentleman, and see in what way these employees may be classified. When the returns are brought down, I will be able to show hon. members who these employees are, when they were appointed, and what their salaries are.

I would like to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to the building used as an armoury at Orillia. In that town two companies have their headquarters, and I find on reference to a local newspaper there, that the building is of such a nature that they are not permitted to store rifles in it, and instead of these rifles being at Orillia, they are kept at the town of Barrie, a considerable distance away. The result is a lack of interest in these rifle companies in the town of Orillia, and I suppose that condition and that result will apply all over the country. I think some system should be adopted of constructing, perhaps, cheap buildings, but such as will serve the purpose in different towns, particularly in places such as Orillia where two companies have their headquarters. May I ask the minister to consider seriously the question of the erection in the town of Orillia of a building that would meet the requirements of the local militia, and one in| which they might store all their arms ?

I have already had that matter under consideration. As I mentioned at a previous sitting of this House, I think it is a disgrace to the country that we have not better provision made for taking care of the rifles of the various companies. I am in favour of adopting a system of erecting a cheaper class of buildings at the various headquarters, buildings which would supply all the needs, and which would not cost a great deal. I think smaller buildings might be used, and yet be quite sufficient for the storing of rifles and other things.
Perhaps the hon. minister would permit me to read an article from a local newspaper of Orillia, which

will give liim an idea of the condition of things there :
The new rifles were issued some time ago, hut they are all stored away at Barrie and it seems they are going to stay there. The rifles will be very useful locked away in Barrie, and in the meantime the soldiers here can become expert shots with peashooters, which will be very useful in time of war. They will likely parade on May 24th with a lath and a butter knife tied on the end for a bayonet.
I think the minister read an item for an armoury at Middleton. What is it to cost ?
The amount spent is $5,501.74, and the total probable cost is estimated to be $8,400.
Was there any difficulty about the construction of the building, or the taking of it over ? There was some statement in the public press that a difficulty had arisen in regard to it.
I do not quite understand my hon. friend. Does he ask if there was some difficulty about taking it over ?
About taking it over-some difficulty, either about obtaining the land or taking over the building. Has there been any correspondence on the subject ?

I think, if my memory serves me rightly, the party we purchased the site from complained that he had not been paid, although the building had been erected. He was getting very angry, and wanted an increased price. The delay was in the Justice Department.
The man thought he was not getting justice.

The matter has now been put through, and it is all settled up satisfactorily. There was some delay in getting the papers to the stage when we could get a certificate from the Justice Department to issue the cheque for the land.
Is it a wooden or a brick building ?	[DOT]
A wooden building.

I observe in the statement of expenditure read by the lion. Minister of Public Works of this sum of $37,120, that no portion of it has been set apart for the erection of an armoury at Belleville. I would like to ask the hon. minister whether it is the intention of the government to provide for that in the supplementary estimates ? I may, while referring to this subject, call the attention of the hon. minister to the fact, which, no doubt, has been represented to him, that within the last year it was found, upon inquiry, that the drill hall, or armoury, in Belleville, which had been in existence for a number of years and which had been occupied by the 15th battalion, had become unsafe, and in consequence of a promise made, the drill hall was demolished, torn down entirely, the battalion being led to believe that a new drill hall would be erected during the present year. I would like to ask the hon. minister whether any provision is being made for that ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Porter) is somewhat mistaken in stating that I referred to the expenditure during the year. An application has been made to the department. It is quite impossible for me to say whether or not there will be anything in the supplementary estimates. Speaking for myself, personally, as I know there is a good bat-tallion and a good militia spirit in the city of Belleville, I would be very glad if my colleagues and the House could see their way clear to granting an appropriation for the erection of a building at Belleville.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Porter) was quite mistaken in saying that there was any condition in reference to the taking down of the old drill hall. There was no promise made. It was taken down because it was condemned by the architect as being unsafe, and it had to be taken down. The question of building a new drill hall is under consideration. I have no hesitation in saying, speaking from my point of view as Minister of Militia, that a new building should be erected, and I shall advise the hon. Minister of Public Works that as soon as it can be done, a new structure should be put up at Belleville.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: While the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) is in his place, I wish to draw his attention to the state of affairs that exists in Gananoque. We had a drill hall and armoury there, and it was taken down without being condemned. A new site was purchased, and we hoped to have had a drill hall and armoury erected on the new site. That was four or five years ago, but nothing has been done yet. A warehouse was rented to store the battery and arms in and they are stored in that building yet. I hope provision will be made in the supplementary estimates to carry out the promise that the government gave when they took down the old drill hall and purchased a site, and that a new building will be erected providing suitable accommodation for our battery and rifles so that the arms may be removed from the place in which they are now stored, because the warehouse is in the middle of a lumber yard and beside the railway track.

There was some communication made to me two or three years ago in regard to some assistance towards an armoury and drill hall in the eastern part of the county of Halifax. I think the sum suggested was a very trifling one indeed. There are some companies organized, or proposed to be organized, in that part of my constituency. I suppose there must be some 25,000 people east of Halifax. The place to which I refer particularly is the Musquodoboit valley. I think some consideration might be given to this request, if there is any necessity, which I believe there is, for a place to store the arms of the men who are in the sendee there. I suppose that this armoury at Middleton is intended for the whole county of Annapolis '1
For the 69th battalion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: How much of it is in Annapolis ?
Part of it is in Annapolis and part in Lunenburg.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The population of Annapolis would be somewhat in excess of that of the district I have mentioned, but it would not be greatly in excess, and I observe that an expenditure of $8,000 is being made at Middleton. Middleton is only a small town of possibly a thousand population, I should think.
I think about that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Of course, the armoury is intended not for Middleton, but for the whole district. Looking at the claims of the district of Musquodoboit valley, I think they might justify the expenditure of a moderate sum of money. I do not know whether the bon. minister has any recollection of the claims which were made by some of the people in that village for assistance. I think he will find some correspondence in his department in regard to it, and I would invite him to give it his attention, because I think it is well to encourage this spirit in the country districts. I know that companies organized in the Musquodoboit valley would be composed of as good material as you could find in Canada.

I do not recollect having received any correspondence such as the hon. member for Halifax speaks of, nor am I aware that there is any military organization in the section unless it is connected, possibly, with the 78th regiment, which has its home partly in Truro and partly in Pictou counties. The city of Halifax" has two battalions, the 63rd and 66th.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: And the Halifax garrison artillery.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext:
Yes. These are all city corps. I will look into the matter now that it has been suggested to me, and certainly my desire is, so far as possible, to provide everywhere a home, or a suitable headquarters for the different organizations of the militia.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax;. My recollection is that there was a small drill hall in Middle Musquodoboit, a number of years ago, which had fallen so much out of repair that it could not be used, and the claim which was made was that a small sum of money should be expended in putting it into such repair that it would be an encouragement for military organization in that district.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I will look it up.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I was not present when the minister read the list of armouries on which it was proposed to spend this money and I did not hear how much he intended to expend in completing the armoury at Toronto. I see that the Minister of Militia and Defence is in his place and I am quite sure that with his co-operation there will be an item in the supplementary estimates to complete the Toronto armoury, if it is not provided for in this vote.

The total of this vote is $9,000 and that would not go far in Toronto. There will be an item under which we can discuss the Toronto armoury.
Experimental farms-new buildings and renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $10,000.
What new buildings are you putting up ?

There will be a new horticultural building at Ottawa to cost $2,500; repairs, Nova Scotia farm, $600; new barn Brandon farm, $2,500; repairs to buildings, $500; Indian Head, repairs, $500; Agassiz, repairs, $400; Total, $10,000.
This must be for an extension or addition to your present horticultural building at Ottawa. Where is the horticultural building on the experimental farm ?
I do not know that I can describe where it is. It is one of the buildings on the farm. The hon. gentleman must have seen it.

You have a place for raising plants and flowers and I suppose this is an extension of that. You take a vote of $2,500 for a new barn at Brandon. I was looking at the buildings there last fall and I thought there was a fairly good building there.

This work is undertaken at the request of

tlie Department of Agriculture as being urgently needed. The chief architect of the Public Works Department has no personal knowledge of the state of these buildings but in view of the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) I will make further inquiries.
Mr. SPItOULE.' I am not complaining of the expenditure if the buildings are needed and I presume they are. I sometimes thought that a more liberal expenditure should be made in the interest not only of the farmers but of the agriculturists throughout the country. I thought there was a fairly good building at Brandon when X saw it last fall.
I shall get the report of the Department of Agriculture and show it to the hon. gentleman.
Is it the intention of the department to erect any new buildings on the Nappan farm.
We have no request this year from the Minister of Agriculture for new buildings.
Are these repairs done by day's work or by contract.
All the repairs are done by day's work under the supervision of the clerk of works of the province.
You would not erect a new barn by day's work.
A new building would be let byt tender and contract.

Is there any change in the policy of the department as to the method of constructing public buildings and doing public work generally ? The hon. gentleman's predecessor took the ground that very many buildings should be constructed by day's labour, and I would like to know whether that is the hon. minister's policy.

At the present time it is the policy of the department to let all public buildings to the lowest tender if it is satisfactory.
Ottawa public buildings, including repairs, ventilation and lighting, furniture, &c., $125,000.
As this is a large item, will the minister give us the details-the different amounts for the different purposes V

I shall be pleased to give the information as far as I have it. This covers general repairs and maintenance in connection with gas, power, lighting, heating, ventilation, closets and fire services. The buildings that have to be maintained are the parliament buildings, the eastern block, the western
block, the Langevin block, the Supreme court, the geological museum, the printing bureau, the fisheries building, and the national art gallery. I suppose my hon. friend does not want the different amounts spent on the different buildings ?
I think the minister might state how much is for maintenance, how much for rents and how much for other services.

The information given to me is not subdivided in the way the hon. gentleman suggests. The work, as my hon. friend knows, is generally done by day's labour, by the staff employed under the architect and the engineer of the department. I can give him the amount expended for wages and the amount for materials.
It was more a question of rents.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rents come in the next item.

There is betweeii $90,000 and $100,000 paid in wages, and about $35,000 for materials, which would include lumber, paints, oils, glass and some furniture. A good deal of the furniture is made in our own workshops by the carpenters and other mechanics. This item also Includes the furniture purchased for the different departments.
What do you do with the furniture that is cast aside ?

I understand that, under the supervision of the present architect, they are making very good use of the old furniture, by making it into new furniture. The policy is of course to collect the old furniture and sell it by auction.
You do not buy the furniture '!
We buy some. The repairs are largely done by our own men, and a good many tables and desks are made by the carpenters in the workshops.
I notice that there has been some change in the system of lighting this chamber. Perhaps the minister will give us a statement as to the cost.

There is no cost for the change of light. As I stated yesterday, a request was made by the electric company to try the arc light instead of the incandescent. I gave them permission to make the test, and I would like to have the opinion of hon. members as to whether the change is more satisfactory or not. For one thing, the new light is very much more natural, more like daylight, than the other.
What change has been made in the system of ventilation ?
The architect says there is no change. It is the same system, but there is a different method of using the blower, the air being brought from the top.
What did that cost ?
The cost was merely nominal, the work being done by the staff of the department.
Did it cost $1,000.

The architect informed me that the total expenditure for ventilation this year, for materials and wages, would be about $1,500. These little jobs are done by the workmen employed in the shops, and no separate account is kept of them.

How is it that the lighting of this chamber is sometimes so much better than at other times ? Sometimes, under the system you are experimenting with, we have a beautiful light, easy to the eyes and very natural, but at other times it is very dim. ' If we could keep it at the degree of excellence we have had it at times, it would be a great improvement on the lighting of last year and a very great improvement on previous years. Is the light on full now ?

Yes, at present I can read very plainly. Of course, this new system is only in an experimental stage, and perhaps when the lamps are put in permanently it will be more satisfactory. But we will give it a little trial before adopting it. I think that the light is an improvement, and if perfected would be much appreciated by lion, members.
Mi-. BENNETT. Is there any uniformity in the purchase of these fittings and furniture ? If not, it is high time that some little economy should be practised and not allow every gentleman who wishes to purchase such articles to get whatever may best seem to suit his taste. Who makes the purchases of office furniture and fittings ?
They are made by the deputy minister and certified by the minister.

It will be well to look into some of these items. I find, on looking over the Auditor General's Report, that there are some fearful and wonderful expenditures. At page 126-V, the Census department saw fit to buy last session two medicine chests at a cost of $6 each. Why should the Census department require these medicine chests. If we are to have medicine chests for every department, we had better buy a job lot at once and get them cheap.
That item does not come under my department. I do not find any item of that kind under the heading of Public Works.

If the hon. gentleman will look at V-126 in connection with the Census department he will find that Mr. Valiquette bought, among a variety of other things, two medicine chests at $6. But if that item is not in the bon. Minister's department, here is one that is. I find that $19.50 worth of gray hair was bought. Was gray hair bought because it was cheaper than red ? That will be found on page V-131.
That could hardly have been the Minister looking for gray hair.

I want to call the attention of the Minister to the expenditure of two of his colleagues. The Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) seems to be a mild mannered gentleman when disbursing the public moneys, for when he wants a desk for his department it only costs $40. But the Minister of Militia is extravagant in his tastes, for I find on Y-129 that he purchased a desk-I presume it was for himself-which cost $155. I have out of my humble means bought a desk for myself and thought that an expenditure of $40 or $50 purchased a very fair desk. I have seen a $100 desk arid thought it something to be envied. But I never saw a $155 desk. Perhaps the bon. Minister can describe the beauties of this article. But while the Minister of Militia has been extravagant, still greater extravagance has characterised another lion. Minister in the purchase of a desk, for I find that in this no less a sum than $165 for one. I know that the House will shudder when it hears who this extravagant minister was. It is no less a personage than the Minister of Labour and the Postmaster General. It is due to the House and the farmers of Ontario that he should explain how he possibly could have disbursed $165 of the people's money, drawn from the pockets of the farmers, to purchase a desk. Before the item passes, I would ask the Postmaster General to rise and give a realistic description of this desk that he purchased with the money of the people of Canada.

At page 131 V of the Auditor General's report, I find an item, [DOT] Goldie & AIcCulloch safe with marble top, 3185.57.' I have never yet had the pleasure of seeing a safe with a marble top. Will the lion. Alinister of Public Works
kindly tell us what is the necessity for a marble top on an ordinary safe, and if it added to the cost to any extent.

I have not the figures at hand giving the difference in cost between a safe with a marble top and a safe with an iron top. But the hon. gentleman having brought the item to my attention, I shall make inquiries among the officers of my department and will let the hon. gentleman know.

It seems that this recklessness of expenditure is to be found in every department of the government. The necessity of having a marble top on a safe, is something that never dawned on my mind until I saw this item. It seems to be about in keeping with the other expensive appointments of the department. This afternoon we had the expenditures on ordinary roller-top desks purchased by the departments. Some ministers, modest in their expenditures, will get a desk at $40 or $50, which, from experience I should think would be a very fine desk. But the Alinister of Alilitia (Hon. Sir .Frederick Borden), according to the public accounts, made an investment of $155 for a desk, and, not to be outdone, the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Alulock) it would seem, had invested $165 in a desk. I assume that that was one of the roller-top style also. I assume it to be only fair to the House and the country, as hon. gentlemen opposite, when in opposition, preached from the house tops that expenditure should he rational and altogether on the same basis as incurred in one's private business, that the Postmaster General should rise in his place and, at least, give a description of the desk, for many hon. gentlemen, like myself, may not have an opportunity for a few years at least, of gazing on tliat wonderful piece of furniture.

I inquired of my deputy since we adjourned at six o'clock in reference to this article of furniture. He informs me that it is not merely a desk, but that it has certain post office additions to it. It is a structure partly a desk and yet it is not a desk, because in addition to being a desk it is fitted up with drawers, files, and pigeon-holes set apart for the different officers of the department, and also for the work connected with the various countries that Canada is in communication with on post office business. The work is classified in these various departments. the respective officers of the department have keys and access to this structure. each going to the portion of it that contains the work coining under his particular charge. It is rather an elaborate structure, but there is great economy of time on the part of the officers, because, instead of having an officer detailed to distribute the various papers and documents to each of the branches which require attention, the

papers are sorted and placed in these various compartments as in a post office and each officer lias access to his compartment.

It is unfortunate that the lion. Minister of Militia and Defence is not here so that we could have a little explanation as to this very expensive desk which was purchased for his department. Perhaps it will be found that it has a whole set of accoutrements attached. The desk of the lion. Postmaster General has a post office attachment, and, therefore, it would only be natural to suppose that the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, who is a close second in the matter of expenditure with the Postmaster General, have a regimental attachment to his desk. I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster General whether it is necessary to have all these particular accoutrements.
The hon. gentleman uses the word ' accoutrements.' I do not know whether he has reference to my colleague, the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, or not.
Yes, I thought you might be able to give an explanation of the matter.

I know nothing about the organization of the Militia Department. If the hon. gentleman's question has reference to my own department. I think I have given the reason why these divisions are supplied. It is for the same reason that you would have compartments, or boxes, in a post office. Instead of having to have officers in attendance to hand out the documents, the documents are classified in these compartments and the various ofli-cers are furnished with keys to them and have access to them. In economy of time and the proper despatch of business this is considered a very ingenious and suitable method.
Where was this desk made ?
I am not able to inform my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) where it was made. We give a requisition to the Public Works Department, and they supply what is asked for.

I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster General whether, in consequence of this labour-saving machine, he has been able to dispense with any of the clerks in the Post Office Department. He has paid a very extensive price for this desk. Of course, if he has been able to save in the matter of the services of clerks and thereby reduce the amount paid in salaries, he might have some justification for purchasing this expensive piece of furniture.
I do not think my hon. friend is serious in presenting a question of that kind.
I notice that the desk was made by the Harris. Campbell & Boyden Furniture Company. Is that a Canadian company ?
That is the name of an Ottawa firm.

I was going to suggest that the sums paid for these desks would appear to be a little high, although they may be good value for the money, the hon. Postmaster General knows that he has under his charge postmasters, especially village postmasters, who complain that their salaries are remarkably low. I would also like to remind the hon. Postmaster General, who is something of a farmer himself, that if he goes into the county of Grey, or into the northern portion of York, the farmers will think that what is paid for a desk would make a fair payment on a farm. They would think this a little expensive.

I have made some inquiries in regard to the purchase of this article of furniture. It is only fair to say to the committee that the item as recorded in the Auditor General's report is somewhat misleading. What is described as a desk, is practically an office for the deputy postmaster general. I dare say the other desk in the Militia Department was for the deputy minister and for the better accommodation of the department in doing its business. This is not a desk, as we understand it-one of those roller-top desks. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said that we may have got good value. I think if hon. gentlemen saw the desk of the deputy postmaster general, they would say that it was a great convenience and facilitates very much the business of the department. Considering the size of the various compartments, and the convenience provided for the holding of papers and the saving of time, I think it will be found a very valuable improvement in the equipment of the department.

I was going to say, while this item was under consideration, that I have noticed several rooms around this House for the use of members, which seem to be rather luxuriously furnished. They have fine roll-top desks and everything convenient and comfortable, while in other rooms occupied by other members, there are few, if any, conveniences at all. I happen to occupy a portion of a room in which there are six or seven of us. There are three tables that would cost, perhaps, $2.25 apiece, there is not a place to lock up anything except within the drawers of the tables and the room is even without shelving of any kind. There are only three electric lamps for seven members and two or three chairs.
I have applied to Mr. Speaker-I am sorry that he is not here to-night, because I am informed that he is responsible for this condition of affairs-for some additional fur-

niture, and he says that the parsimonious economy insisted on by this government is such that he cannot afford to give me any more furniture.
An economical government.

Noticing the very handsome outfits which ministers have in their departments and in some of the rooms about this House-and I am not saying it by way of grumbling-I think we might fare a little better nevertheless if we do belong to the opposition. I asked Mr. Speaker if he could furnish a little cupboard or anything where we could put papers away.
You want an ice box.
What is tickling the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) now.
You ought to have an ice box.

I have no doubt whatever that my hon. friend will profit very much by his advice if he will take it to himself, so that he will keep himself moderately under control. I think this is hardly fair. It does seem to me that when we are here to do the country's business we ought to have some more conveniences for doing it in our rooms than we have.
You will be there for a long time. You ought to have more accommodation.

That is an argument in my favour. I am drawing the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works to this matter because his predecessor was always very good to us. I know that when we applied to him for anything he always tried to meet our views, and I know his liberal and generous successor is quite equal to the late minister. I hope he will take note of this and that he will profit by this discussion.

I really think the accommodation provided for hon. members of this House is small enough. The members ought to be entitled to such furniture and lamps as the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) has referred to so that they can do their work with some comfort. I know it is a great advantage for a gentleman having to attend to correspondence and other business to have a desk which he can lock up and find his papers in order when he returns. If an application were made for furniture, sucli as the hon. member referred to, I feel satisfied that the House would be very willing that it should be granted by the department. I quite agree with what the hon. member says as to the desirability of having these conveniences for hon. members. Only one or two hon. members have come to me and I have only been too glad to supply their wants in that direction. There is, of course, a limit. The
amount of the vote is based upon a fixed expenditure, but there is always a margin for the purpose of supplying these conveniences each year. I shall be glad to give every application I receive the consideration it deserves, and so far as I can, help to increase the comfort and convenience of the members.

What is done with this furniture which must be accumulating in large quantities in the different buildings ? Every year there seems to be extensive purchases, and still the members of the opposition find it impossible to get anything more than a plain table, in fact they cannot get a cabinet or a desk. I suppose there must be occasionally a cleaning out of these departments; what is done with this old funiiture after the purchase of new furniture ? Is it sold at auction ?

The great bulk of this new furniture has been bought for the new buildings, new rooms that have been made during the last two or three sessions. There was no old furniture to store away. The business in the different departments has increased so much that we have to rent buildings outside, and some of the furniture has been used in them. As I stated before six o'clock, in case of a room that was refurnished, if there was an old table, or desk, or anything of that kind past usage, it was sold by auction. Latterly, as I explained, the man in charge of the carpenters has been taking some of the old furinture to the workshop and having it made over by the workmen under his charge. Any that is of no use is sold by auction. But these new purchases that are made, most of them, are to furnish some half a dozen new rooms that were opened during the last recess.

On referring to the Auditor General's Report of last year I find a startling state of affairs revealed. If the general public of this country were aware of it they would be filled with amazement when they are told that it costs every day of the year, on the average $300 for looking after these buildings. Referring to page Y-120 I find that there was spent last year for labourers and carpenters about these buildings, $00,530. Turning to the next page I find that there was paid out for a staff to oversee these men, no less a sum than $8,220. Further down there is a so-called mechanical staff costing $20,410. It is a startling fact that it costs $100,000 a year for the maintenance of these buildings. I have not the figures of a few years ago, but I cannot believe they ever ran up to such immense amounts ns this. Tt is about time that the pruning knife should be applied. As to furniture it must be plain to any man who knows anything about it that it must be a most extravagant desk that costs $105. You go on through this expend!-

ture and what is revealed ? Chairs costing $12 or $13 a piece. I suppose it is the old story of having a good time for the first time in your life. That seems to he the rule followed throughout these departments. Every page of this Auditor General's Report shows that there is a most reckless and extravagant expenditure in every department of the government. This expenditure ill becomes gentlemen who for years made the burden of their song some little trumpery, trivial, petty expenditure that a decent man would have been ashamed to mention.

Is there any portion of this money being spent to fit up offices outside of the main building ? I understand there are several buildings in Ottawa rented for the use of the government; is this money being used to fit up those buildings as well ?
When a building is rented and furniture lias to be procured for the staff, the Public Works Department is called on to furnish the necessary furniture for these rooms out of this vote.

What proportion of this was used for that purpose ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, About $35,000.
Mi-. SPROULE. Was any portion of it used for the census staff ?
It would include repairs done by our own staff ?
On page V-131 I see an entry : ' W. C. Edwards Company, Limited, biack walnut back for book case, $50.' Would the minister tell us what the front of that book case cost ?
The deputy minister informs me that he thinks that must be a misprint. It probably means a black walnut book case.

How are these supplies procured ? Are they bought from time to time on an order from the department, or is there an effort made to procure them all at once by asking for tenders for the articles required ?

In some cases when there are a number of articles to be bought, tenders are asked for them, but as a rule they are bought by the architect's branch from the different manufacturers and dealers as the case may be.
Are prices asked for ?
Yes.

There seems to be a great number of desks and ofiice chairs bought for the different departments. There is an 1 Mr. BENNETT.
account here for decanters and tumblers, and absorbent cotton even, which some years ago would have been made a text for a sermon by our friends opposite.

Since they have opened up the bar in the restaurant, and now that the temperance question has died out, and the referendum has been defeated, we must expect them to furnish the bar. We were exempt from those items for some years, but I suppose we must look for them in future.
That must have been a mistake ; it must have been for a water bottle.
At page B-135, of the Auditor General's Report, there is an item for a ' pair of crutches with iron tips.' What member of the cabinet got the crutches ?
One of the carpenters was seriously injured, and the department thought it only fair to do something for him, and among other things he was supplied with crutches.
The minister promised us before dinner that he would explain that item for ' $19.50 worth of gray hair.' Has the minister had any light upon it since the dinner hour?
My hon. friend will have to take my word that the gray hair was not for the Minister of Public Works, but for some of the other members of the cabinet.
I will accept the explanation that it was for some of the baldheaded members.
The system is to keep a regular list of everything that is purchased from time to time, and if anything is disposed of, which is not very often, that is entered.
Is there any system by which the government take stock annually of the goods which they have on hand ?
I do not think it has been the custom to take stock annually, but the books would show for a number of years, when an article was purchased, from whom it was purchased, and so on.

An enormous quantity of these things has been purchased for the

last five years, and there should he some system of tracing these articles and knowing whether they are on hand or not.

We are constantly furnishing new buildings on account of the increasing business of the country. There may occasionally be an item for replacing furniture which has worn out, but the great majority of these articles were purchased to supply new offices to accommodate the increasing staff which is necessary to carry on the increasing business of the country.

The business of the country is certainly growing at an enormous rate, and naturally you have to extend your buildings and you have to furnish them. Instead of having a few thousand dollars for this expenditure, as we had some years ago, we have now a few hundred thousand of expenditure. In view of this, it is not out of place to say that you should have some way of taking stock of the quantity of furniture and the enormous amount of stationery that you must have on hand. Thousands and thousands of dollars worth of stationery are used every year. An ordinary merchant would keep an account, not only of his stock in trade, but of his furniture and other assets as well, and why should not the government conduct its business in the same way ? It might give some trouble, but it would be a safeguard for the public, and it would be consoling for honest employees to know that they had the same furniture in their offices at the end of the year that they had at the beginning. The minister would do well to start a set of books which.would show what furniture and what stationery is on hand. I do not know where all those beautiful fancy goods come from that are distributed among the members every year. I think perhaps that is an item that might be very well dispensed with. I do not like to find fault with it, because having taken them and kept them, I am possibly not in a position to do so, but there must be a great many thousand dollars expended in that way every year, and I think we might dispense with that. Under these circumstances, I think it would be well to keep stock of the quantity bought, the quantity disposed of, and the quantity on hand at the end of the year.

My hon. friend's suggestion is quite proper, but I believe that each department has an officer for the special purpose of keeping track of the stationery. I know that in my department I could not get a lead pencil myself without applying to the officer in charge of the stationery. Honourable members will admit that one could not make an estimate of what it might cost to maintain and equip and keep in proper order the buildings which we have in Ottawa. I think it is a fair criticism, however, to
say that we should see that we get value for what is expended; and if any purchases are not proper or the prices paid are not fair, I would be only too pleased to have them brought to my attention at any time. I have not had sufficient experience to say whether the system is as perfect as it might be; but I may say that there is nothing particularly extraordinary in this vote, because I find, on looking over the totals for many years back, particularly to 1879, that a great deal more had been voted in previous years than we have at the present time. But I will look into the matter and endeavour to see that proper books are kept, so that we may keep track of the purchases and avoid waste-so that we may see that only purchases are made of such articles as are required, and that we get value for the money expended. The cheapest article, as my hon. friend knows, is not always the most economical for a permanent institution, and due regard should be had for the service got out of it.
Does the government insure all the furniture it has, or take the risk itself ?

None of the departments carry any insurance at all. The government carries its own insurance in all the departments, except in case of some special contract; but after the contract is delivered, we carry our own insurance.
If you carry insurance, you would have to keep stock, otherwise in the event of fire you would have no way of establishing your claim.
As the Minister of Militia and Defence is now here, perhaps he will give us an explanation of this very expensive* desk which he has purchased.

I have not had an opportunity of looking up the matter, and was not aware of having purchased a desk of this kind. I have no doubt a requisition was made to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works for a desk, and he probably thought that the importance of the Militia department and the excellent work that has been done there justified the purchase of a desk in accordance with the importance of the department. This is the first intimation I have had of what that desk really cost. I am not able to give a very full description of it. It is a desk and table combined, a very handsome piece of furniture, and I shall be very glad to have any of my friends on the opposite side of the House, or any others, call and see me there, and I will show them the desk. That is the only explanation I can give at the present moment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
It seems that we are to judge of the importance of a department

by the gorgeousness of its furniture. According to that standard the department of Agriculture is a very mean department, because the desk of the chief officer there only cost $35 or $40. If the Minister of Agriculture were back from the east, it seems to me he would not be pleased with the explanation the Minister of Militia and Defence has given as to why his desk is so much more expensive and gorgeous than that of the Minister of Agriculture. I suppose it was not on account of the honours which have been showered on the Postmaster General and the Minister of Militia and Defence lately that they had to tone up their departments.
They had to oil up.
I am glad, however, that we have had some sort of explanation from the Minister of Militia and Defence.

I notice that the Secretary of State also seems to be indulging in luxurious appointments, because when he dangles his feet on the floor, they rest on a rug that cost $45. May I ask if the Secretary of State has show'll a disposition lately to indulge in other extravagances, by making further requisitions ?
I have not had any requisitions lately from the Secretary of State. I think he must be supplied now.
What is the real necessity for spending such an enormous amount on labourers ? $90,000 seems to me a great deal of money to spend on labour in connection with repairs and maintenance.

Of course, the number of buildings that have to be taken care of is pretty large. They are the Senate, the House of Commons, the Governor General's Secretary's office, the Privy Council, the Department of Justice, the Auditor General's office, the Department of Finance, the Secretary of State's Department, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Indian Affairs, the Department of Militia and Defence, the Department of Customs, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Inland Revenue, the Department of Public Works, the Department of Railways and Canals, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of the Postmaster General, the Library of Parliament, the Supreme and Exchequer Courts. It is a pretty extensive institution to look after. Iam not prepared to say that there are not more men employed than are really necessary. We keep a certain number employed from year to year, and at certain times we engage temporary help. The officers in charge of these men are all under the jurisdiction of the chief architect, in whom we all have a great deal of confidence, and I Mr. FOWLER.
am sure that if he were aware that more men were employed than were necessary to attend to the work, he would report the fact to the department.
How many men are employed ?
There is in the neighbourhood of one hundred all the time in the employ of the department at Ottawa.
What is being done about lighting ? I have noticed that occasionally this session the lighting is very bad.

As I explained before recess, the electric company asked for the privilege of making a trial of the arc light instead of the incandescent, and we have allowed it to do so. It is not going to cost the country anything. We have drawn the attention of the company to the fact that the lighting is not regular, but it has been very good the last few days. It is merely an experiment, and the great majority of the members think it an improvement.

What do the electric lights in the buildings cost ? Some years ago we went into that question at considerable length, but the plant then had not been installed, and we could not get definite information.
Two dollars per light of sixteen-candle power per annum.
That is a very high price for a number of lights. In many of our country villages, we pay very little more, and of course, use fewer lights.
I will have an inquiry made into the matter and see if we cannot make some reduction. The average price I find is about $4, but we have a contract for a number of lights at $2.
You can get lights at $3. In our village we only pay $2.25.
In the town I come from it is not that cheap. It costs about $50 a year for eight lights.
It costs $3.75 per light per year at Three Rivers, where there is abundant water power.

They are sold right in our place at $25 per year for eleven lights of sixteen-candle power each. In some places the charge is even lower, and a portion of the time the electricity is supplied by steam. Throughout our part of the country, I could count up many towns where the charge is below $3.
For a continuous light?
Not all night. Only until 12 o'clock, and then on again at 5.30 a.m., but we are offered an all night service for the same price by another company.
Usually in small towns they pay by measure.
We pay a flat rate per light, and there is no meter at all. Will the hon. minister be good enough to tell us what he is doing about improving the ven-tillation ?
The ventilation will cost something like $1,500. There is no change in the system, but we have added some apparatus for pumping in fresh air, which I think is an improvement.
In some places about this building, you occasionally use gas as well as electricity. Is it the same company that supplies both ?

No, separate companies.
Rents-Dominion public buildings, $33,500.
Does this cover all the outside rents ?

$14,500 is the total amount for leased buildings. I think that out of that item the city of Ottawa is paying something over $30,000. Glancing the items over, I am pretty well satisfied that it runs over $30,000 in Ottawa. I shall have to ask a sum in the supplementary estimates. This is $33,500, but the total in the departments is $44,500.

Some announcement was made a short time ago of the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite as to the erection of another public building in Ottawa. It would be a good move to procure the necessary land and put up a decent building. The government would save money, instead of paying this enormous sum in rents every year. Has the hon. minister any statement to make as to the erection of a new departmental building ?

Not at the present time. But I quite agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke). Not only would we save money by putting up a new public building, but we should have far better facilities for conducting the public business than at present. Of course, I have been in the department only a short time and have had a good deal to do. But before the session is over, I hope that, with the assistance of the officials I may be able to prepare something to propose to the House to remedy the difficulty we are now labouring under.

I hope the Minister of . Public Works will carry out this resolution and lay before the House a plan for a
new building. Every year for the last three years when this matter has come up we have had the same answer-that the matter would be taken into consideration. I find that, in looking over this list, for instance, that the building used by the census commissioner and his staj was to cost a rental of $3,000, according to the statement of the cx-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). A few days later, in bringing down his estimates, by some mysterious process, the rent had doubled, and was $6,000 instead of $3,000. The then Minister of Public Works called down his deputy minister for not having corrected his first statement. In looking over the expenditure, I find that this item has again increased and is $0,500, instead of $6,000. I notice other peculiarities about these rentals. For instance, here is an item for $2,000 paid to the Misses Thistle for two years rental. I cannot understand why rent for two years should appear in this account. In several instances this crops up.
That was the rental of a building that was rented as a matter of urgency by the Department of the Interior.

Referring to the building used by the census department, may I ask the Minister of Public Works, in view of the fact that the department are not only paying $6,500 a year, but that last year they spent upwards of $10,000 in improving the building, is that $10,000 to be deducted from the rent or has any agreement been made under which that amount is to be paid back partly or altogether ? It seems almost incredible that the government while paying this enormous rent-for it is an enormous rent, for capitalized it amounts to $130,000- should expend about $10,000 in repairs and improvements.
Under the arrangement that has been made, improvements made by the department are not allowed for.
Can the hon. minister tell us how much longer they are going to use the building-how many years before the term for the lease will expire ?
I am informed that the lease is terminable at the option of the department at the end of any year.
And, on the other hand at the option of the landlord also ?
The deputy minister informs me that he would have to bring down the lease to be sure of its terms. But it is terminable at the end of the year at the option of the department.

It seems strange that the department should conduct matters on

this basis. In tlie first place an enormous rent is paid, and then $9,000 or more is spent in repairs. If I understand the items, and I think I do, the department have actually installed a system of hot water or steam heating-which is it ?
The MINISTER <#' PUBLIC WORKS. A system of hot water heating. _
Can the minister tell us whether it is intended to make any more expenditures on this building ?
There is no intention of making any changes or improvements in this building. If repairs are needed during our occupancy of the building we are liable for them.
Were any repairs put on the Thistle building ?
No.
Why was the rent increased from $6,000 to $6,500 ?
I may say that $6,500 is the amount of the rental under the lease.

When this hot water system was put into the building, were there any arrangements made that at the end of the government's term of occupancy that system could be taken out again ? Surely it is not intended to present these people with a system of hot water heating in addition to this large amount of rent. I cannot imagine such an arrangement being made in a business matter. Some arrangement should have been made for taking out this hot water system. Second hand radiators are as good as new. If the system was to be put in, arrangements should have been made to allow of its being taken out again.

There was no arrangement on the subject. The building had been occupied for a good many years and the system of heating, I understand, was suitable for the occupants of that time. The building was rented by the Department of Agriculture and fitted up by the Department of Public Works for the purpose for which it is used. But the heating was not satisfactory. Many of the rooms had not any heat at all. So, the department put in a new system of heating.

I can well understand that, when men were working in these rooms the rooms had to be properly heated. There is no objection to that. But there should have been an arrangement that the government could take out the system when they left.
Was it any part of the terms of the lease that the government should spend $9,000 in improving the property ?
I understand that the terms of the lease provided that the government had to make any changes or improvements they required for their own purposes.
And though not obliged under the terms of the lease the government have spent $9,000 in improving the property.
No, they simply did this because they found it necessary in order to make the place suitable for the staff to work in.
How long will these buildings be required for the purposes of the census ? Is it expected that the census will be completed before the next one is taken ?
I shall have to get the information from my hon. friend, I could not give it off hand.
Is this building used exclusively for that purpose ?
So I understand. I have never had the pleasure of being in it.
I understand it is not the intention of the minister to renew the heating apparatus for this building. How about the furniture '! Will they leave the furniture in ?
The furniture comes under a different head. We will move that out, of course.

It would be interesting to know if the interest of the country has been preserved in another way. In the new Ontario Act there is a provision concerning landlords and tenants that if the lease is drawn in a certain way the tenant can, at the end of the term, remove all the fixtures. Perhaps the minister could inform us if there is a clause in the lease which will enable them to remove those fixtures at the end of the term ?
I have not got the lease here, but I have not the slightest doubt that the interest of the public has been safeguarded In that direction.
Will the minister have the lease brought down ?
I will have a copy brought down.

The other day we had a statement of the cost of the census up to date. Would the minister tell us if, in that statement, are included the rents that are paid for these outside buildings that are used exclusively for census purposes V

They are not included in the cost. The *
