rents are paid by the Public Works Department out of this appropriation, and would not be included in the expenditure of the other department of the census.
How much rent has been paid up to date for the use of these buildings for census purposes exclusively ?
During the three years that this building has been used for census purposes, the rent would now be about $19,500. That is the one building that we pay rent for which is used for the census.
Is that charged up to the item for taking the census ?

No, it would not be included in that.
Rideau Hall, including grounds, renewals, improvements, furniture and maintenance, $17,000.
I am glad to see the Postmaster General in his place, because in 1895 or 1896, I think, he made a very strong speech about the extravagance of the government at Rideau Hall.
Get the speech and read it.

I have read it, it is a very good speech, and it would have been very much in the interest of the country if this government had lived up to the sentiments of that speech. If they had torn down the old building and built a new one, it would have been in the interest of the country, because the buildings are not very ornamental, and I should judge are not nearly as comfortable as they ought to be for the money expended on them. I have been looking over the expenditure under this head for the last three or four years, and it has been almost enough every year to build a decent building. In 1899 we spent on that building in the way of furniture, additions, repairs, &c., $29,736 ; in 1900, $24,991 ; in 1901, $31,249.11 ; in 1902, $14,012. I see in the estimates for the coming year, $28,000. Now I think in one of these years they built a new addition to the hall at an expenditure of about $40,000. I think this is a very lavish expenditure, and something ought to be done to stop it. My hon. friend when in opposition took very strong ground against this expenditure. I believe he was acting Minister of Public Works during the absence of the late minister in the old country, and he was in charge when there was a very large expenditure. Had the hon. gentleman began when in office to carry out the principles he laid down when in opposition it would have been better for the country.

My hon. friend is confounding my views with his own. I do not think he will find that I ever discussed the expenditures at Rideau 32
Hall. I did discuss a feature connected with the Governor General, but I did not, so far as my recollection goes, discuss the internal economy of that house. He suggests that the expenditure on Rideau Hall was especially high during the time I was acting minister. I was acting minister for a few months in 1900, and during that time it was my duty to carry out certain works, not originating during my temporary occupancy of the office, although I share the full responsibility for them. Those works consisted, among other things, of the thorough underdraining of the building. The hon. gentleman will be surprised to know that the drainage of Rideau Hall was so defective that the water lodged to the extent of several inches, and sometimes a foot, in the cellar, and it is a wonder that many lives were not lost. It became necessary to construct drains, much of them through rock, which made the cost very high. I saw myself the condition of affairs in the basement at Rideau Hall, and I am sure my hon. friend would have been one of the first to say that such a condition should not be allowed to continue. I presume, like others, he occasionally shares in the advantages that that institution affords. But when he presses us to be economical, I would refer him to his colleague the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule)-I was going to say the minister ; I hope some day he will be minister. It is only a few moments ago that that gentleman was complaining of our economy. He wanted us to spend more money.
I was surprised at that.
I was surprised too ; nevertheless he shows that he is becoming more enlarged In his views, and I would commend his example to my hon. friend.

I will undertake to furnish the speech made by the Postmaster General if this item is allowed to stand. I had occasion at one time in this House to quote extensively from it. I have a vivid recollection of the criticisms that he offered on that occasion.

I do not think I discussed Rideau Hall, but I have discussed the classes of expenditure the hon. gentleman is now discussing. I have explained that during my temporary occupancy of the department there was a large expenditure for drainage, and an additional building, which became necessary. If the hon. gentleman were to visit it, lie would see the need of it, and the need of furnishing it. The late ex-Minister of Finance was familiar with all the circumstances connected with the furnishing and the expenditure, and he did not see anything in it to take exception to. He asked a question or two across the floor of the House, and when he learned how the expenditure



was carried out, without so expressing himself, by his dropping the subject, he satisfied me that he was perfectly content with the expenditure.

How does the hon. gentleman explain the next year ? If they left Rideau Hall in such a good condition for $24,000 or $25,000 a year, why was it that the very next year there was over $31,000 spent on it ?
I Was not there then.

No man can evade the responsibility of the government if he is a member of it. The expenditure was cut down next year to $14,000, but this year it has gone up to $28,000. My recollection is that the hon. Postmaster General did not only criticise the expenditure of Rideau Hall, but be also criticised the number of cabinet ministers and he also objected to the' Governor General's salary. He made a comparison between the cost of the government in the United States and of our government in Canada showing that they had only eight ministers while we had fourteen. We have not heard him saying anything in that direction since he and his party took office.
It is a growing time.
Yes, it is a growing time and I say that these hon. gentlemen are benefiting by the growing time, but that does not excuse them for having failed to carry out what they advocated while in opposition.

I do not know whether I have any sins to answer for, that were committed while I was in opposition. I had the same views then that I have now. There is a certain class of criticism that is legitimate, and it perhaps matters very little to the public who have to pay the bills what any hon. member has said either on the opposition or on the government side as to the actual facts of the money expended. What I want to draw the attention of the Committee to is that I have been looking into this matter a great deal and have gone back fifteen or twenty years. I find that for some reason the department has not been quite frank in regard to the expenditure on Rideau Hall. So far as I can find out it costs the country about $25,000 a year to maintain Rideau Hall and that from time to to time smaller estimates have been brought in than were required with the result that accounts have been running over and debts have been accumulated. I think that parliament and the people are entitled to know what the actual cost of maintaining and furnishing this place is. I do not, as a minister, wish to come here and submit an estimate pretending to maintain Rideau Hall for less than it is possible to do it. If, on carefully looking into the matter with the Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
officials of the department, I think any saving can be made I am quite willing to try and make it. I am quite willing that any hon. member on either side of the House should point out the fact if he thinks that any undue or unnecesary expenditure has been made in this connection. As I have just taken charge of the department, I thought that I should come frankly to the Committee and tell them what it has cost the country for a great many years to maintain this place. It is my intention to ask the Committee for an additional expenditure to clean up the back debts that exist and I say it frankly to the Committee that the maintenance of Rideau Hall will cost about $25,000 per annum.
What has been expended on an average for 20 years on this ramshackle place ?	[DOT]
$25,000 will pay the interest on three-quarters of a milion dollars at 3.per cent. Surely it would be better to put up a building for $250,000 and stop this leak.
You would have to maintain a larger building at greater expense.
This of course includes the cost of the maintenance of the grounds. It is not all for additions or improvements.
There is $8,000 for heating.'
No, not for heating.
A modern building would save half of that on the heating alone.

There would be $3,000 for the maintenance of the grounds. I do not think they are kept up extravagantly in comparison with private grounds even in Canada and certainly not in comparison with public grounds in other countries. The grounds could not be kept in the state in which they are for much less than $3,000 a year. Hon. gentlemen in this House know from their own experience that much smaller grounds cost a great deal of money to maintain them properly. Unless there are other items in which some saving can be made I want the Committee and the country to know that it takes the sum I have mentioned to maintain Rideau Hall and it has taken that for a great many years.

I think we are all agreed that Rideau Hall should be kept up in an efficient state or rather in such a state as will be creditable to the country as a whole. What my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has suggested is a

subject that was passing through my owu mind. The expenditures on additions and improvements and repairs to this building during the past twenty years must have aggregated an enormous amount. Is it not a fair question for the hon. Minister of Public Works to ask himself whether it would not be in the interest of the country to tear that building down and erect another that would not require so mubh money to maintain. It seems that $8,000 a year for lighting and heating a building of that kind is absolutely absurd. In my limited experience of such things I should consider it altogether out of the question, although I do not doubt it has been expended, and is necessary to be expended in the present condition of the building. If you have spent $100,000 in additions and improvements in the last ten or fifteen years, and I dare say you have expended that sum, that sum itself would put a good modern building which would not be so expensive to maintain as this one. I do not believe very much in this policy of patching up an old building and adding to it from time to time, and in the end having still an old building difficult and expensive to maintain.

I want to refresh the hon. Postmaster General's memory as to the statements he made in 1895-
These sums are .quite beyond the resources of the people of Canada. We have disbursed annually during 25 years an average of $21,785. and in addition $4,754 for furniture for Rideau Hall.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would tell us how the resources of the people of Canada will stand an annual expenditure of over $30,000 which he will stand up and defend to-night while condemning a smaller expenditure under the administration of the Liberal-Conservative party in 1895.

My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) has read the answer iu the light of the circumstances under which I made the observation. He says that in 1895 I expressed the opinion that $21,785 and $4,754 was too much for the then resources of Canada. I was speaking in 1895. We are now in the year 1903. Canada is a different country under a Liberal government from what it was in 1895.
Hear, hear.
I am glad that my views are concurred in by the hon. gentlemen opposite.
The patches on the farmer's trousers are as bright to-day as they were then.
Is this the policy that the hon. gentleman advocates that when the revenue of the country is larger the government propose expending more on furniture and other things at Rideau Hall ?
The hon. gentleman had better make his own speech.

I would like the hon. gentleman to give us an explanation how it was that he condemned in -this House an annual expenditure of $25,000 when the Liberal-Conservative party was in office while now he stands up and defends an expenditure of more than $30,000 per annum for the same purpose.

I should think that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) is an observer of the times and if he is he can supply the answer to himself. The condition of the country in these days was very different from what it is now. We then had an unprogressive party in power; they paralyzed the trade of the country and it was necessary to be economic at every point, even to the extent of hampering the public service. With the limited revenue of the country at that time you were plunging into debt-do you want me to make a campaign speech and explain it all to you. You know the state of the country and of its finances in those days and you know the state of the country and of its finances to-day. We can now afford to manage our affairs more in harmony with the requirements than we could then, and as long as the present administration is in office and its policy produces such happy results the country will be in a position to deal in a more progressive spirit all along the line.
The letter carriers will come in then.

The letter carriers and all classes will benefit. During my regime it has been a great pleasure to me to improve the status of the letter carriers over what it was when my friends opposite were in power.

It is refreshing to hear the Postmaster General talk about the condition of the country in view of the fact that in his own department they will sell you a postage stamp that you cannot use in the ordinary postage business. What did his department do to inflate his revenue. Some time ago they sold the jubilee stamps to a denomination as high as $10, and if to-day you take one of these $10 stamps to any post office in the country they would not even exchange it for two cent stamps. That is done to inflate the revenues of the Post Office Department.
It makes the country look like two cents.

The Postmaster General has made a comparison between 1895 and the present day justifying large expenditure now because of the growing time. I take it that in 1895 this country was willing to pay whatever was necessary for the keeping up of Rideau Hall. The prosperity of the

country or anything like that has nothing to do with it ; it was and is simply a question of keeping up that property in a fitting manner for the Governor General of Canada. The Postmaster General when he was in opposition complained that it took $21,000 a year to maintain the property in a fitting manner for the representative of our Sovereign, but he now spends $30,000 a year in doing that identical work.
And not doing it as well.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) has misapprehended my speech. If he will read the speech he will find that I spoke of nothing else except as to what the country could afford. Looking at a comparison of our revenues, the country could not afford to do then what perhaps it ought to have done in this matter. It can afford now.

The Postmaster General seems to misapprehend the situation entirely. The hon. gentleman from Peel (Mr. P.iain) quoted from a speech of the Postmaster General a strong denunciation against his predecessors in office because of the expenditures in connection with Rideau Hall. When the Postmaster General came into office he found that the expenditure for a quarter of a century averaged $20,000 or $50,000 a year, but the Postmaster General and his colleagues who have been presented to us as a good business administration are spending $30,000 a year. If there was any business about them they would erect a modern building that would be much more economjcally maintained.

What
price.

Say $500,000 if necessary, and at three per cent it would cost you $15,000 per annum. The Postmaster General now justifies an annual expenditure largely in excess of the expenditure made by his predecessors which he denounced at the time. I venture to say that if an examination of Rideau Hall were made to-day, it is in no better condition than when he came into office when it was maintained at a much less expenditure.
Oh, yes, it is. It is a different building altogether. It is the difference between white and black.
That old building ought be pulled down and a new building put up and if the hon. gentleman would advise the doing of that he would be saving money to the country.
Perhaps so.

It must be apparent to every one who has visited Rideau Hall that it is a waste of money to spend $.30,000 an-Mr. BARKER.
nualiy in trying to keep up that aggregation of old apartments. It is my opinion that it is the duty of the government to make the necessary provision to put up a decent modern building.
Would we not be at the expense of maintaining that too ?
It certainly would not cost so much for maintenance as the old building does.
What is the cost of maintaining the city hall in Toronto ?
That is a different matter altogether.
It is expensive enough.

The city was obliged by the grand jury and by legal process to put up a court house and it was thought that a saving would be effected if both the court house and the city hall were under the same roof. That is an extravagant building but the city was forced to make the change because of the action of the grand jury and of the judiciary.

There is not the slightest doubt but that if we had a new modern building a considerable saving would be made in the annual maintenance especially with regard to heating and lighting. I do not think there would be a very great deal of saving in other directions. It would be much more satisfactory as my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) says if we had a building more creditable to the country. However, we are dealing with the item as it is before us and I felt it my duty, after an examination of the expenditures for some fifteen or twenty years to ask for a vote according to the expenditure in the past. These estimates were prepared two or three weeks after I came into office and I have since found that it will be necessary to bring a supplementary estimate equal to the average cost for the past few years. It is only fair to say that out of this amount some $3,000 was spent for maintenance of the grounds. I do not think that is extravagant; I think that must be fairly well managed. The question of putting up a new building is one well worthy of consideration. It would give greater satisfaction no doubt to the occupants and to the people of the country. The maintenance could be reduced somewhat, not very materially, but perhaps about twenty-five per cent, unless that new building would bring around some new expenditures that we do not think at the present time. The aggregation of old and patched up buildings that are there now certainly cost more for maintenance than would a modern building. I wished the House to know what the actual

facts have been and there is no use deceiving ourselves with regard to the maintenance of these buildings. As long as I occupy the office I shall invite criticism as to whether or not that money was properly expended. If I find that any reduction can be made I shall endeavour to make it, but the experience has been that for fifteen years it has cost about this amount to maintain the property.
The sum of $33,500 is paid by the government every year for rents. I suppose some of that will be dispensed with when the census is completed, if it is ever completed.
My hon. friend was not in when I gave the explanation of that. The total amount we pay in rents throughout the Dominion is $44,500. In the city of Ottawa we pay in round figures about $30,000.

That represents, at the rate of interest which the government is obliged to pay, about $1,000,000. There were discussions during the past session as to the erection of another building ; and it seems to me, if that were done, some economy might be effected. It has been suggested that there is some difficulty in regard to a site. I think the government has plenty of land for the purpose of another building without buying any more land. There is a site where the Supreme Court building is now, affording plenty of room between Bank street and the location of the conservatory for a very large and suitable building-a building that would be an ornament to the grounds, and would afford accommodation for many offices, besides having the additional merit of providing a suitable room for the Supreme Court, which is very badly housed at present, and suitable accommodation for the library of the Supreme Court, which is now in a disgraceful condition for lack of room. I would like the minister to take this into consideration. I know that a great deal of dissatisfaction exists on the part of members of the bar who come to Ottawa with the accommodation provided for the Supreme Court. In addition to that, I may suggest to the Minister of Public Works that we have really enough space in the buildings now at the command of the government to carry on the business of the country if that space were properly economized. I do not suppose it could be, because the buildings have been constructed in a different way. But my hon. friend has, no doubt, been in some of the great buildings in New York, such as the Produce Exchange, in the basement of which many clerks are provided with all the accommodation they require in a comparatively small space. If a building were constructed where I suggest, I believe the annual expenditure of the country could be reduced, and the Supreme Court could be housed and many offices Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
provided, in such a way as would do credit to the country.

When looking at the estimates this afternoon, I must confess that I was very much surprised at this vote of $30,000 for rent of extra offices. I do not require to go back a long way in my memory to recall the time when the members of the present government were sitting on this side of the House, and when they made the corridors ring with their shouts about the extravagance of the Tory party in filling all the public buildings in Ottawa from cellar to garret with civil servants, and when they used to picture to the farmers of the country how they were robbed to support such an extravagant lot of civil servants. They made them believe that the buildings here were so full of civil servants that they were almost forcing the roofs off. Are the buildings too full now ? Yes; the census staff used to be in the Langevin block, but now it is in a large building by itself ; then the models were moved out; and now the building is filled with officials from cellar to garret, and the government are paying $30,000 a year to rent other buildings. Can you say, you are another, you did it too ? I recollect very well that a gentleman who is now relegated to a sublimer sphere-and we know what contempt the hon. Postmaster General used to have for members of parliament who accepted offices of emolument-used to visit my constituency and find fault with the extravagance of the Tory party for expending more money on Rideau Hall ; he even complained of the cost of washing the napkins. Now the Postmaster General tells us the country can afford it. Is that the way a prudent farmer manages his business ? When his finances are buoyant, does he not first take the mortgage off his farm instead of indulging in greater extravagances ?
We can never afford extravagances.

You just keep still. You told an hon. member to make his speech. I am making mine. I want to tell the hon. Postmaster General that he is there to answer questions that we ask, and not to put questions in my mouth. The hon. gentleman thinks he is the monarch of all he surveys, his right there is none to dispute ; but I look on the hon. gentleman as the people's servant, and he should recognize that fact, and not attempt to dictate to me what I shall say. I am here to answer the very bold and extravagant charges which the Postmaster General used to make. What is his policy ? The policy of the Conservative party, which he used to say was bleeding the people white. Now it is a buoyant revenue, and the extravagant expenditure is only a liberal one. How things have changed. I wonder that the hon. gentleman does not have remorse in his sleep, and wake up crying, 'The Lord have mercy on me for my hyprocrisy.'

In the expenditure for Rideau Hall, at page V-144 of the Auditor General's Report, I see this item :	J. A.
Teasdale, 12 pillows, at $3, paid twice, $72. This is an Rem that ought to he explained. I may say, with regard to the question of a new building, that if this matter had been looked at in a judicious way some years ago, before the expenditure referred to by the hon. Postmaster General had been made, it might have been wise to consider the question of pulling down the present buildings, and erecting more suitable ones. But in view of the fact that within very recent years, large additions have been made to these buildings, I do not think this is the time for us to consider the question of going into increased expenditures. I submit whether the reduction in the annual charges would be such as to justify our incurring an expenditure of a very large amount. In this account are a great number of items that would not be lessened by the putting up of new buildings. In fact I am inclined to think that if we went to the expense of erecting new buildings, that would involve the expense of new furnishings and fittings and a variety of expenses which we are not able to anticipate at present, and there would still be the ordinary annual charges as great, or perhaps greater, than they are to-day. ' It is to be regretted, whether we attribute it to the present government or preceding governments, that the advisability of putting up more modern and compact buildings was not considered years ago. But having regard to the large expenditures made in extensions within a few years. I do not think it is well to have the idea go forth that we are contemplating the expenditure of a very large sum to put up entirely new buildings.

The hon. minister has said that $44,500 is what is paid in rents, out of which $30,000 is paid in Ottawa. Will that $14,500 cover all the rents paid throughout the country ? Does it include the various post offices for which the government pay rent ?
It includes all the department pays.
Does that mean post offices ?
If we rent any post offices it does, but I do not think we do.
There are several small towns where there are no government buildings and in which the department gives an allowance to the postmasters for rent. Is that included in. the $14,500 ?
The Public Works department have nothing to do with these post offices. This is for rent paid directly for public buildings throughout the Dominion.
I wanted to distinguish between what the Public Works department pays and what is actually paid by the government of the country.
I am not aware that the government of the country pay any other rent.

I certainly have not made myself plain. There are several post offices throughout the country, which are not government buildings, and for the use of which the department makes an allowance to the postmasters for rent. That, I presume, is not charged up in this $14,500, but comes out of the Post Office department.

We make an allowance to a postmaster for supplying the department with office accommodation. We have nothing to do with keeping it in repair. The postmaster supplies the boxes and collects the rents, and we make a rental allowance to him for supplying us with accommodation.

That is the point. But I do not want it to go forth that the government are paying only $44,500 for rents. I think it is much larger. Take the city of Ottawa. You have $30,000 charged for rents. Is that a fixed rent liable to last a number of years, or are the leases affecting certain buildings on which the government pay rent liable to cease soon, and thus the rents be decreased ?

It is likely to increase to meet the demands of the various departments for increased accommodation. I have refused in several cases, and tried to get along with the accommodation we have. In connection with the large immigration into Manitoba and the North-west, the business of the Department of the Interior has so increased that more place is urgently demanded to carry, it on. I would not like to say that I see any prospect of decreasing the amount of rent unless we put up a building of our own.

The government should consider the advisability of erecting a building, because it is a well known fact that the high rate of rent paid to parties in Ottawa for the use of their buildings is altogether in excess of what it ought to be. Would it not pay the government much better to buy land and erect a building ? Even if that should cost more to begin with, it would be a source of economy in the long run. That item of rent, instead of decreasing, is liable to increase, and I think it would be a proper policy for the government to erect public buildings of its own. I judge from the remarks made before recess that the government are considering the advisability of erecting some building.

While I did not make any definite promise

before six o'clock, I promised to bring in a report before the close of tlie session as to what I thought should be done in this direction. It will cost a considerable sum of money, and it is wise that we should have an opportunity of carefully considering the plans, &c., before making any recommendation. I think it is a matter we must' deal with as quickly as possible.

If we are ever going to have the census completed, the building in which that work is being done might well be dispensed with. I have always thought it was a most extravagant rent for the government to pay, namely, $30,000, for some ten years for that plain building, four stories high, on Medcalfe street. I do not think that it is nearly all occupied, and surely. if the census is ever to be completed, we might save that $10,000 or $15,000 rent we have to pay on that building.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This item was passed half an hour ago.
And I would draw your attention to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Public Works has been answering the questions we have asked on the subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know it. But the question under discussion is ' Rideau Hall, $17,000.'

Is the minister prepared to answer the question I asked with reference to the item paid twice ? At the same time, I might call attention to another item of the same class-the eighth item on page Y-114, two mats at $3.50 each, paid twice, $7, extended $14. It seems that there is some mismanagement in this affair. Apparently, the accounts have not been looked after carefully, when, on the same page we find in two places items which admittedly have been paid twice.

A careful audit showed that these amounts were included twice and the amount was refunded. I will have a memorandum from the accountant's branch giving full inforifia-tion of how this occurred.
Rideau Hall-allowance for fuel and light,
Surely the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir Wm. Mulock) will have something to say with regard to this.
I have always supported this item. I think my record is all right on this.
What kind of fuel do they burn there, Mr. Chairman ? This is a dreadful expenditure.

My information is that some years ago-1 think during the incumbency of Lord Duff-erin-an arrangement was made with the
Governor, which has been continued ever since, that, instead of furnishing fuel aud light, the government was to make an allowance of $8,000. We pay that over to the Governor.
I was not aware of that. This is a mere matter of book-keeping, then. As a matter of fact, His Excellency gets $8,000, and the amount is charged to heating and light.

Was that sum allowed when the Postmaster General moved his memorable resolution to reduce the salary from $50,000 to $35,000 7 I am not aware whether the Minister of Public Works voted for the resolution or not.
Could the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) give me the date 7 According to my recollection, and to the information given to me now, this arrangement was made in Lord Dufferin's time.
I remember the vote. I voted against the Postmaster General's resolution. I think it was in 1892 or 1S93.
This arrangement was made previous to that.
When was this agreement entered into to pay this sum of $8,000.

During Lord Dufferin's time-twenty-five or thirty years ago.
Furniture-Dominion public buildings, $12,000.
Is this to furnish new buildings the government is erecting outside 7
This is for furniture for all the public buildings throughout the Dominion.
Has it anything to do with the Ottawa public buildings 7

No. If the hon. gentleman cares to know how the amount is expended, I may give the summaries of expenditure for last year : Nova Scotia, $704 ; Prince Edward Island, $63 ; New Brunswick, $1,112 ; Quebec, $1,800 ; Ontario, $2,500 ; Manitoba, $847 ; North-west Territories, $423 ; British Columbia, $944. These expenditures are up to 1st January last, and make a total of $8,490.
As there is a small balance on hand, is it the intention to pay some of the accounts that are outstanding 7

I should be sorry to know that there are amounts not paid. I am afraid that the departments, including the Department of Public Works are a little careless in paying accounts. This arises from the system of taking too small a vote and not having

enougli to pay for tlie services of the year. That I do not approve of-it is bad policy. If there is money to the credit of the account, I will pay outstanding amounts ; if not I will ask for a supplementary vote and pay them.
There is a balance left unexpended ?
There was on the first of January.
Is there any since ?
There is probably a small amount.
I should be glad to call attention to a small item or two that might be paid.
I should like to know when the salary of Mr. John Frawley, caretaker of the Orillia public building commenced at $300 per annum ?
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) put that question when the item is under discussion under which that salary is paidV I will then give the information.
Very well. The comment I wish to make is this-
My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) will excuse me, but we are soon to reach the appropriation out of which this salary is paid.
Very well.
We have reached the foot of the page, and perhaps the hon. minister does not propose to go further.

We are now at the general item No. 124. I think we had an understanding that so many nights having been passed on these votes, this one should be passed. This applies almost altogether to the Ottawa buildings.
Of course, many hon. members are absent, this being Friday night.

1 would be willing to reserve the right of any hon. gentleman to make any remarks he wishes regarding this, whether it passes or not. But there is no item here, so far as I know, that will not be included in the supplementary estimates for 1902-3. So, there will be the same opportunity for discussion that there is under these items. My hon. friend will notice that these items refer to the Dominion public buildings at Ottawa. But there are two or three items besides, upon which the discussion might be resumed.
Ottawa public buildings-heating, including salaries of engineers, firemen and watchmen, $67,000.
Does this include fuel purchased by public tender ?
Yes, it includes fuel for the buildings at Ottawa alone.

What was the cost last year ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS The votes for many years past have been taken in a very unsatisfactory manner, one year's expenditure running into another year's expenditure. But so far as I can ascertain from the department, it costs about $85,000.
This business administration will lose its reputation if it permits this condition of affairs to go on much longer, allowing the cost of one year to dove-tail into others.

This is a somewhat serious matter, and I would appeal to the members of the Committee on both sides to treat it as such. The system has existed for a great many years. This government is perhaps just as responsible for allowing the system to continue, as was the preceding government for initiating it, that Is, taking votes too small, and carrying the expenditure over into another year. I would like the assistance of hon. gentlemen on both sides in remedying this unsatisfactory condition of the accounts.

Under the circumstances, I would suggest that the Committee rise now, and in the meantime the minister can give his attention to this serious matter, as lie admits it is. We have made substantial progress to-night.
I appeal to the hon. gentleman to allow me to put this vote through.
We should have to get all the particulars of the prices paid for this coal, to whom paid, and how much was bought, and how much is owing to each person now. i

This item might be allowed to go through, because there woud be abundant opportunity for discussion on other items. I want the fullest investigation made into these accounts by the officials of the department; but they must have time, and hon. gentlemen must remember that the officials are here from three o'clock in the afternoon till all hours of the night. I assure the leader of the opposition that this matter will come up again, and can be discussed, and full explanations will be given. There is nothing to be gained by letting this vote stand.

I am sure we lmve uo desire to interfere with the operation of the department by keeping the officials here to an unreasonable hour at night. In view of the statement made by the minister that before the final disposition of the estimates he will bring down all this information, personally I have no objection to the item passing, i
I think the minister could give us a good deal of this information now.
I was going to state to the House that I have conducted an investigation for a number of years, and I find that a special vote has not been taken to meet this item.
A regular slip-shod method.
Somewhat.
Do we understand the hon. gentleman is going to bring down the amounts paid, and from whom the coal was bought ?

I am prepared to give that information now; for the present year. I find this system has been going on for a' number of years, taking a small vote and every year expending more than we have voted. There are two objections to that system. In the first place, we have not a clear knowledge of what we are expending for this purpose; secondly, we cannot do business in a satisfactory way without getting somewhat near a correct estimate of the vote that is required. The contract for the supply of coal for the present year was let to John Henay & Co. The prices were :	Furnace coal,
$6.45, egg coal. $0.50, stove coal, j$G.50, blacksmith coal, $6.

In what season of the year were tenders asked for ? Because if you apply early In the year you are in a position to get your coal cheaper ; whereas if you wait till late in the season, it will cost more.

Last year the advertisements for coal were sent out in May ; this year the advertisements are out now. I do not think that it is necessary to make the contract earlier in the season than April or May.
Is this per ton of 2,000 pounds, or per long ton ?
Per ton of 2,000 pounds.
The price seems to be a pretty long price.

If my bon. friend had the responsibility of furnishing the coal under the contract he
would not think so. I must say that the Ottawa contractor stuck to his contract, unlike dealers in other places in the Dominion and furnished the coal at the price at which he had agreed.
The coal would be ordered in the summer, I presume.
I do not know when it was ordered, but the contractor here has been delivering right along every week, or month, as it was required and is doing so yet at the price agreed upon.
What quantity does he supply under the contract with the government ?
Six thousand four hundred and twelve tons were called for under the contract.
What system have you of weighing the coal ? Is it left in the hands of the company that sell it or do the government have an inspector ?
It is weighed on the government scales and checked by our own man.
There was some wood, was there not ?
Yes, 276 cords of mixed hardwood at $4.75 a cord-very cheap.
Will the hon. minister read the prices of the coal again ? It was all anthracite coal, I understand ?
All anthracite coal.
Is there no bituminous coal used in the buildings at all ?

My hon. friend refers to the coal that is used in the grates. This grate coal costs $7.70 a ton. There is no bituminous or soft coal burned in the furnaces of this building ; that is all anthracite. We paid for grate or cannel coal $7.70 a ton.
And for the anthracite coal ?
Six dollars and forty-five cents per ton.
And there was another item of $6.50 a ton.
That was for 200 tons of egg coal ; soft coal, $6.50; blacksmith coal, $6. There were only twelve tons of that.
Would the hon. gentleman tell us when the contract was made ?
In May last.
May, 1901, or May, 1902.

This is an outrageous price to pay at that season of the year. I got my own coal for that and I did not put in a thousand tons of coal the same as the government did. Did you call for tenders in Ottawa to supply the departments with coal, and if so, what was the lowest tender ?
We called for tenders.
How many tenders were received ?
I have not the names of the tenderers here, but six tenders were received last year.
And this was the lowest ?
Yes.	%
I must say that the government is paying a pretty high price by contract for coal.

We were fortunate in having a contractor who delivered the coal. I am sorry to say the tenders this year are much higher. We advertised in the public press for tenders. It is a nice large order, and I do not see why coal dealers in any part of the country should not put in tenders. My hon. friend is perhaps comparing the price we paid with the price at the place where there is a very much lower freight rate than there is to Ottawa. There is a very great difference in the freight rates between here and Toronto for instance ; that is from the anthracite field. We take only anthracite coal from Pennsylvania. If the hon. gentleman will compare the price we have paid with the prices of coal in other cities, he will see that it is a reasonable price.

I am prepared to admit that if you made the contract in May, 1902, and did not have it delivered until December of that year, the prices are all right, if the contractor carried out his agreement. I know that many dealers did not carry out their agreements throughout the country generally. If he carried out his agreement and he was to deliver the coal during the summer months, comparing the price with that in other places, then, the price is high. Of course, I do not know what the freight rates are. I am only judging the price from that prevailing in my own locality.
It is understood that we are to get all this information.

I will bring down all the information when I ask for the balance of this vote in a very short time.
Ottawa public buildings, elevator attendants. $9,000.
What does this mean ?

That is to pay the cost of running the elevators in the public buildings at Ottawa-in this building, the east block, the west block, in the Langevin block and the census building. In the parliament building there are four elevator attendants, and they get $45 a month each. They are striking for higher pay.
They are not getting too much if they are only getting $45.

I am glad to hear the hon. gentleman say that; they have been bothering the life out of me. In the east and west blocks there are three elevator attendants, in the Langevin block one engineer, one fireman and six elevator attendants, and in the census building one elevator attendant.
How many are there altogether ?
Fifteen.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if there is an attendant in connection with the elevator service in the Seybold block. What did it cost to Install the elevator there ? Is it an electric elevator ?	[DOT]
Yes, the department put in an elevator at a cost of about $2,000.

That gives us rather a shock. I did not find that in the other expenditures, and it will be a tribute to the department over which the hon. gentleman presides, that not only have they installed a hot water service, but that they have put in an elevator service for the owner of the building. Certainly this is a business administration.
Ottawa public buildings, gas and electric light, including roads and bridges, $24,000.
After looking into this item I think that this sum of $24,000 will cover the lighting.
Then the cost of maintenance of the Ottawa public buildings must be more than $200,000.
The $125,000 was for installation and work in connection with ventilation and lighting; for materials used and work done.

But still one is rather staggered at the aggregate of all these amounts. Leaving Rideau Hall out of the question I see the following items here :	$125,000, $67,000, $9,000, $24,000.
$7,000, $8,000, $5,500. There is nearly a quarter of a million dollars which seems to be pretty large for the mere upkeep of these buildings.	.

Since I came to the department I have been

making every possible investigation with a view of finding out how the money was expended. X am anxious to make a saving if I can, and X wish the House to have full information as to the actual cost.
What is the actual cost ?

In this particular item this will cover the cost.
6; Secretary of State, 5; Senate, 4; Trade and Commerce, o. Total, 223.

In the minister's own department there are thirty-eight telephones. Are they working overtime or how do you come to have so many ? I cannot expect the minister to be familiar with the location of the telephones in the other departments, but perhaps he could tell us where the thirty-eight telephones in his department are located.
Ottawa public buildings, telephone service, 57,000.
I do not know whether room sixteen has a telephone or not, but I think room six should have a telephone.
There is no telephone in room sixteen; some think it is necessary but I do not think it is.
There is a telephone in the Liberal whip's room, but there is no telephone in the Conservative whip's room.

When I had the honour of being whip along with the present occupant on the other side of the House, we always applied mutually for any advantage and I was not aware until this present moment that there was not the same privilege given to the opposition whip as to the government whip. So far as this House is concerned a grant to one party should be equally given to the other.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.
If the chief whip of the opposition desires a telephone and the government whip has one I certainly shall feel it my duty to grant the request.

How many telephones are in use in these buildings.
. The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. We have 223 telephones in connection with the departmental and parliament buildings.
I appeal to the minister if that is not an enormous number. Why, if you had one in every room I don't think that there are 223 rooms in all the buildings. Are there any outside ?

The following is the number of telephones : Department of Agriculture, 14; Auditor General, 3; Customs, 5; Dominion Police, 8; Finance Department, 3; Government House, C; Geological Survey, 3; House of Commons, 34; Indian Affairs. 3; Inland Revenue, 9; Department of Interior, 39; Department of Justice. 1G; Department of Labour, 1; Mounted Police, 3; Militia and Defence, 20; Marine and Fisheries, 8; Ottawa River Works. 3; Post Office, 8; Printing Bureau, 5; Parliamentary Library, 4; Privy Council, 30; Public Works. 38; Railways and Canals,
I have not made myself familiar with them, but I have been looking into the matter somewhat.
I think it would bear investigation.
Is it not a fact that many of these telephones are in the private houses of the officers of the department.
That would apply to the ministers and deputy ministers and to the chief officers.
In the Privy Council Department not only has the minister's secretary got a telephone in his house, but the assistant to the secretary has one as well.

In a growing department like the Department of Labour there is only one telephone and in the important Department of Finance there are only three, and they seem to get along with that number. It seems unreasonable that we should have thirty-eight telephones in one department. It appears to me that it requires some explanation.

In the Department of Labour there is one telephone and one chief officer, but the bon. member will admit that in the Public Works Department it is reasonable to expect that the deputy minister, the chief architect, the chief engineer and the engineers in charge of outside work should have telephones. I shall look into the whole matter. In fact the list is on my desk now and under consideration to see if there can be a saving made, but I cannot promise a saving because I do not know what the conditions are.
Out of the total of 223 telephones how many are in the public buildings and how many outside.

There are 13S inside and eighty-five outside. It does not necessarily follow that they are in dwellings, but they are outside of these grounds. I will bring down a full list, so thnt the hon. gentleman may see them for himself. I may mention an application which I had to-day. We fitted up the third floor of the House of Commons. A great many members attend the Railway Com-

inittee on that floor from eleven to one; and it was represented to me that it would be a great advantage to the gentlemen, I think on both sides of the House, occupying the rooms on that floor, to have a telephone. I do not see how the minister can refuse that request. Some of these telephones are sessional.
I was not aware that gentlemen having rooms for their private convenience were asking for telephones. I was not aware that there were rooms for gentlemen belonging to both sides of the House.

I did not say that. I said that we fitted up these rooms, that they were occupied by gentlemen on both sides of the House, and that they applied for a telephone. However, that will come up when I submit the list.
Ottawa public buildings-grounds, $8,000.
Is that for the maintenance of these grounds ?
Yes.
Are they maintained by contract or by day labour ?

By day labour. We have a foreman in charge.
Major's Hill park, $5,500.
There is an increase here of $1,000. Wliat is the reason of that ?

The increase has been asked for because it was found that the amount previously voted did not meet the expenditure. There has been a new building erected there, and perhaps the park is kept up better than it used to be. Half of the salary of the superintendent is charged to this account, $720 ; there are two gardeners at $40 a month, and seven labourers at $35 a month, for nine months ; new plants, seeds, water system, manure and contingencies : making up the $5,500. 1 do not see very well how the park and the buildings cau be maintained in the state they are in now at much less cost. I have looked over this item, and I think it desirable, while we have charge of the park, that it should be kept up in as good a state as at present ; and we ask this amount rather than overdraw the account.

I think that is the proper policy, and it does not appear that the gardeners and labourers are paid too much ; their salaries are very small. If there has not been sufficient money voted, where do you get the money to pay these accounts, or do you have to stand off the men until the money is voted by parliament ?
That is the usual way, and it is a very poor principle.
Does the hon. gentleman get Treasury Board orders ?

No.
Salaries of engineers, firemen, caretakers, &e., Dominion public buildings, $99,000.
I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works when the salary of John Frawley, caretaker of the public building at Orillia, commenced at $300 per annum ?
Will the hon. gentleman let me take a rnein-I orandum of that and give him the information on Monday? I have not the information here.
Then I will ask the hon. gentleman another question : Does he propose to pay to John Frawley $300 next vear as the caretaker of that building ?
Is he a new appointment ?
He lias been there a year or so.
The matter has not been brought to my attention before.

I have no fault to find with the payment of the salary ; but I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the whole matter of the caretaker of the Orillia public building. A man named Baskerville was appointed by the late government, about 1893 or 1894, to perform the duties of that office, I think at the same salary of $300 per annum. There was a by-election in East Simcoe in 1S97, when the Postmaster General came into the riding and camped there with his camp followers ; and, smarting bitterly under the defeat administered to him by the electors of that riding, that hon. gentleman came down here bound to revenge himself on any person and every person who had assisted to bring about that defeat. It was shown to him that there was a caretaker in the Orillia public building who, in all probability, having been a Conservative, had voted for me ; and forthwith his decapitation was proceeded with. It was utterly impossible to show that the man had not discharged the duties of his office well, or that he had in any way interfered in the election beyond the exercise of his franchise as a free man. What happened ? He got peremptory orders that he was to vacate the building. When the matter was brought up here in the House of Commons, the then Minister of Public Works informed the House, as the debate at that time will show, that he had decided on a new line of policy in regard to the Orillia public build-

ing In accordance with the wish of one of his colleagues ; and the line of policy that he pursued was this, that the caretaker's services were to be dispensed with, and for the future the postmaster of the town would have charge of the building. That was simply a means to an end. Though it was utterly impossible to formulate against the man a charge of inefficiency or of having interfered in the election, he was thrown out by the Postmaster General's instructions- because he was the minister who had charge of that district, and to whom the then Minister of Public Works referred in very plain terms as the colleague whose instructions he was endeavouring to carry out. A little later, this Mr. Frawley-and I have nothing to say derogatory of him, because I believe he discharges his duty all right-was installed. And in order to give a little appearance of decency to an intolerably indecent transaction, he was kept down there for a limited time at the small salary of ?10 a month. But when the hon. gentleman thought sufficient time had elapsed to work out his little scheme, without too great a shock to the public, Frawley was given the same salary as that paid the former occupant, Mr. Baskerville. If ever there was a miserable display of party spitefulness, it was this. Smarting under the defeat which he had met in the riding, he took this roundabout way to gratify his little vindictiveness and put this man out of his position. But this man is still alive and recording good Conservative votes in East Simcoe, and the minister's treatment of him will stand as a disgraceful monument of party spite and mean vindictiveness.
The observations of the hon. gentleman from East Simcoe, so far as I have any recollection of the matter, are utterly without foundation.

I would simply ask the hon. minister whether it is not the case that he was in that riding and conducted a campaign and that he came back smarting under defeat, and that the man whom he appointed to fill the office formerly held by Baskerville is receiving the same salary as Baskerville was paid. When I remonstrated with the hon. Minister of Public Works at the time in his own office, he asked me not to blame him, that it was too small a transaction for him to take in hand, but that orders had been given him from another quarter. That quarter I knew, however, was the quarter occupied by the Postmaster General himself.

It is hardly necessary for me to repeat my contradiction. I have no recollection of ever hearing of the existence of the man to whom the hon. gentleman refers. I do not think that the circumstance ever occurred such as the hon. gentleman describes of my
having been a party to turning this man out of office. I do not think I ever heard of his existence before to-night.

I would like to ask the hon. the Postmaster General if, when dismissals are made throughout the country, as mauy have been, without any charge having been preferred, these dismissals are made with his knowledge or do his officers take it upon themselves to make them. 1 would like to know from the hon. gentleman whether in all cases these dismissals are made) with his knowledge and approval. I am now speaking more particularly of cases where no charges were preferred, and the man was simply told that his services would cease on a certain day and some person be appointed in his place.
Is the hon. gentleman alluding to postmasters ?
Yes.

Witli regard to postmasters, it is my duty to know of every dismissal or removal from office. I have no doubt that I authorized every such transaction ; but whether I did or not, I assume the full responsibility. Occasionally, one of my colleagues has been acting In my absence, but I presume he would only do what I would have done myself if present. It may be assumed that I have authorized every removal which has taken place.

I am very glad that the Committee and the country should know the position which the hon. minister takes. But I fear he would scarcely stand on a crossroad in this country, and make the denial he has made to the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett). I know nothing about the particular case to which the hon. member for East Simcoe referred, but I know of other cases so small and so mean that I hesitated coming to the conclusion that the hon. minister had any knowledge of them. He says now that he has knowledge, or even if he has not, he takes full responsibility. Well, I know of many cases where men were receiving small salaries and were simply told to go. No complaint was made against them, their public service was good, but some persons conspired to turn them out and the minister dismissed them. The country will be shocked at the hon. gentleman's statement to-night. He takes full responsibility of these dismissals from one end of Canada to the other and then makes the most flat denial of a case of dismissal which occurred in East Simcoe.

My hon. friend asked me about post offices, and the case in East Simcoe was that of the caretaker of a public building. I take full responsibility for every removal from a post office. If the hon. gentleman desired to be fair with me, he would give me the cases

to which he refers and discuss each case on its merits. He would then be able to judge whether I was warranted or not in the course I took I am prepared to justify every removal of a postmaster that has taken place. I think the hon. gentleman will find that I have protected the postmasters. He will find that his remarks will not have the sympathy of the Conservative postmasters, and that I have made very few chnuges in the vast army of postmasters who were in office when I took charge of the department.

I may say to the hon. gentleman that I intend drawing his attention to some cases concerning which I have the correspondence and which will bear out the statement I make to-night. The hon. gentleman has told us that the Conservatives have been very well treated because he has permitted them to occupy their positions. That is the substance of what he has said.
That is the return I get for treating them well.

All that the Postmaster has the right to demand of any postmaster, whether Liberal or Conservative, is a fair, and honest service, and if a postmaster, who has given this service is permitted to retain his position, he is simply getting just treatment. If any postmaster whether Liberal or Conservative is not doing his duty fairly, he should lose his office. But so long as he does his duty, he should not be discharged, and I do not see that the hon. minister is entitled to any particular credit for not having discharged such a man. He has told us that Conservative postmasters will say he has treated them well. Has he given them exceptional 'treatment ?

In many cases I have stood by them when I would be quite as well warranted in removing them from office. I have always given them the benefit of any doubt. I have always favoured the postmasters in office. I would like the hon. gentleman to inform me of any particular cases in which he thinks injustice has been done. The removals have been very few indeed. In the western provinces, the removals have been infinitesimal, and that I presume is the section of the country to which the hon. gentleman refers. There have been grounds for removal that were in my discretion ; and I think I have in all cases leaned to the side of those who were in office. My hon. friend has a neighbour who has had some experience of my practice.
Do I understand that the Postmaster General is prepared to discuss now the removals he has made ?
When the proper time comes-not now.
We will discuss it when the time comes.

As I have been referred to, and as I desire to do what is fair by both sides in the discussion that has arisen,
I may say that my brother is postmaster in St. Thomas, he was suspended and a thorough investigation took place. He was reinstated and paid his full salary while out of office. I think the Postmaster General was fully satisfied that the complaint was not warranted, and for that reason he reinstated him.' I think the Postmaster General did justice, and I am prepared to give him credit for doing justice after investigation. Also the postmaster of the city of Windsor was suspended. I do not know the details of the investigation, but I know that the result was that the postmaster was reinstated. Of course, I know that, when the government came into power in 1890, by a ruling they made, certain persons who were appointed to office within a certain period previous to the change of government were dismissed. In the town of Aylmer, in my own constituency, Mr. D. H. L. Price was appointed by the Conservatives as postmaster. He served several months under this administration, then he was dismissed and another put in his place. No fault was. found with him, but the reason for his dismissal was the ruling which had been made, providing for the dismissal of those appointed within a certain time of the Liberals coming into office. These are the facts, and I state them candidly.

On the 24th April, 1899,
I asked the question :
1.	Who is the caretaker of the public building at Orillia ?
2.	When was he appointed ?
3.	Upon whose recommendation ?
4.	What salary is paid to him ?
The Minister of Public Works of that time answered the questions as follows :
1.	John Frawley. 2. Fourth November, 1898.
3.	Frawley was the man employed by the former postmaster who was at the same time caretaker, to do the cleaning of the building. It was found that he performed his work very satisfactorily, and that was the reason why he was appointed caretaker. 4. $15 per month.
Now, every word in that bears out the statement I made a little while ago, that after the dismissal of Baskerville, who was the former occupant, the work devolving upon the postmaster, the Minister of Public Works appointed Frawley as caretaker at $15 a month. My recollection was that it was $10. No man of common sense will believe that the then Minister of Public Works had any animus against this man Baskerville, and I challenge the Postmaster General to show that there is in the Department of Public Works any complaint against him for having been derelict in the discharge of his duties. And I here say, and say without reservation, that the report

of the debates will show that the Minister of Public Works, when endeavouring to explain why he had dismissed Baskerville, plainly intimated that it was by reason of political pressure brought upon him by a colleague. The Postmaster General will not deny that he was in that riding-as he had a perfect right to be, and as I have no doubt lie will be again. Every one knows that each minister has a certain portion of the country of which he takes charge for campaign purposes, and these constituencies are in charge of the Postmaster General. 1 leave it to any man of sense on the other side to say whether it was vindictiveness and spitefulness on the part of the Postmaster General that brought about that dismissal of Baskerville, or whether it wa s because the then Minister of Public Works sitting in his office, knowing nothing about the matter, made up his mind, for the reasons for which nobody can divine, that Baskerville ought to be decapitated. I shall place the statement of the Postmaster General before the people of Orillia, and I do not think they will have a very high regard for his veracity.
Has the appointment of caretaker for the town of St. Thomas public building been made yet ?
No.
There is an increase in tliis item of $10,000. Why is that ?
The department is taking over the caretaking of post office buildings of Montreal and Toronto, 'and it also has six new buildings to. take charge of during the coming year.
How was the caretaking for Toronto and Montreal paid for before V

I believe the caretaking was very unsatisfactory. It was done by the Post Office Department. We are in a better position probably to look after that sort of thing, having the clerks of works, who will hire the men and have the work done properly. Great complaints were made that the offices were not properly cared for.

By how much will that reduce the expenses of the Post Office Department ? The Postmaster General has been boasting of a surplus. He started with a surplus, but came out with a pretty heavy deficit before he got through with the Auditor General's Department and the Finance Department. His Newmarket story is pretty threadbare. How much would this reduce his expenditure 1
I do not know exactly-a few hundred dollars.

My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) knows that the vote has not been increased in accordance with the service. There were sixteen new buildings added to the list last year, and this year there were six. I am not prepared to say what the saving would be to the post office department in our taking over Montreal and Toronto. The complaint of the officials was, apparently, that the work was not done at all. Perhaps my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) can speak about that.
I was going to ask the hon. minister if there were any complaints on file. I never heard of any complaints of dereliction of duty on the part of the caretakers. Have the officials complained ?
Yes, there was a letter written by the post office inspector regarding the state of the building
That letter will be brought 'down ?
Yes.
Who was the post office inspector who complained ?
I don't remember now. It was done at the request of the department, on the complaint that he was not keeping the post office in a proper state.
I want to understand this thing. I understand the minister to say that a saving to the post office of about $200 was effected by the change.
No.
Then how much could be saved by transferring this expenditure to the Public Works Department ?

I am not prepared to say just how much it will cost to keep the post offices at Montreal and Toronto in a proper condition, perhaps a few hundred dollars a year. Some labour will have to be employed, some charwomen. We are not taking these over for fun. Representations were made officially to the department of the necessity of assuming this charge.
I do not want to object to the change being made if it will result in economy. But must there be a new caretaker and more persons employed in this post office at Toronto ?

Some of these caretakers have been urgently requesting a little increase in salary. Many of them get less than $400. They complain bitterly that they cannot support themselves and their families on their present salary, and a small increase of $25 or $50 will be given to some who appear to be underpaid.

The caretakers appear to have almost absolute control over the public buildings, and this remark applies to the departments of Inland Revenue, Post Office and Customs. I think the caretaker in each building should be subject to the orders of the head of his department. They should receive instructions to keep their places in proper condition. In our district we have found that the caretakers will not take their orders from their superior officers.
Some resolutions reported.
